title: Matildas legend enters arena of greatness in milestone match
text:
It was almost imperceptible.

The slightest shake of her head as Steph Catley listened to Matildas coach Joe Montemurro describe her as one of the world's best footballers.

It was as if she disagreed with the label. But there is no disputing the veteran defender's standing in the game.

She is among the world's elite and one of Australia's greatest ever, as a player, leader, and humble champion.

Against Colombia in Canberra tomorrow night, she will become just the seventh Matilda to reach 150 caps; three other members of that club are in this squad.

"This team feels like my family. We've grown up together, and I'm honoured every single time I touch the pitch with these girls, and I wear that jersey," Catley said.

"So 150 times is massive, and I'm very, very proud of that."

Steph Catley says it's special to reach the milestone at home. (ABC News)

Catley has been at the heart of this generation that has driven women's football in Australia at full throttle, from the shadows into the spotlight.

"I think the work that the previous Matildas have put into this team and women's football has been incredible," she said.

"But this group has done so much for the game, for this team, for women's sport in general.

"There's still a long way to go, but what we've achieved so far has been incredible."

Catley is a fierce presence on the pitch, whether playing for the Matildas or Arsenal, and, at 32, is still very much in her prime.

Steph Catley has been a mainstay of the Matildas' defence for over a decade. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

But when she took the time to reflect on her career, the tears welled up in her eyes.

She said the emotion made it hard to talk about, but she regained her composure and did it anyway.

"I'll never take it for granted that I'm able to represent this team and play for my country," she said.

"And even representing Arsenal, it's everything that I dreamed of as a kid. It's everything I've worked my entire life for, and 150 caps is massive.

"And you do get to a point where every day gets a little bit harder on your body and mentally. But I think being around the girls and the fact that we are like a family … I want to be the best version of myself for them.

"That's what drives me, I think, and my family as well. They're all the way over here in Australia, and I've played overseas pretty much my entire adult life.

"So those sacrifices are big, and I think you want to make it worth it in the long run."

Steph Catley says her teammates and family drive her to keep going. (ABC News)

Montemurro has been a constant in the Catley journey, from coaching her in the A-League Women, to Arsenal, to the national side.

His affection for her as a player and person is clear.

"I've had the honour and the pleasure of working with what I think is one of the world's best footballers, but more importantly, as a person," he said.

"We should be proud as a country to have someone of the calibre of Steph Catley in our midst and growing up and hopefully still with us for a while.

"But what she's given on the field and off the field, I think, has been absolutely special and very unique in the world of football."

Steph Catley has captained the side for extended periods during Sam Kerr's various absences. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Catley, like so many members of this Matildas' golden generation, has achieved so much but is still missing a major international trophy.

Her tearful interview after losing the Women's Asian Cup final in March was filled with the feeling of a missed opportunity.

Time has helped reignite the fire to try again.

"We really could have won that tournament, so I think that was tough for us to take," she said.

"It just builds that hunger for the next chance that we get, another step to build towards what we want to achieve."

title: $5m home which sold after a week believed to be record-breaker
text:
The most expensive house on the market in South Australia's Riverland has sold, achieving what is believed to be a residential sales record for the region.

The almost 5,000-square-metre property sits alongside the River Murray in Renmark with 450 metres of river frontage, five bedrooms, four bathrooms and 11 carport spaces.

It was listed for sale for $5 million and was taken off the market within a week.

The property was last sold in 2011. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

While the exact price the new owners paid is unknown, it is believed to be 10 times the median house price in Renmark of just above $450,000, according to online property business REA Group.

Some agricultural properties have sold for tens of millions of dollars, but real estate agent David Kanizay, who sold the home, said its connected land and building quality helped inform the price.

"Without a doubt, it's a highlight for my career," he said.

When questioned ahead of the sale, Mr Kanizay said the home's quality spoke for itself.

David Kanizay says the property is one he will remember forever. (Supplied: David Kanizay)

"You don't put values like that on property unless there's a justifiable reason why, otherwise people will just laugh at you," he said.

"But no-one's come to me and said, 'That's ridiculous.'"

Property data company Cotality found homes in regional South Australia take an average of 49 days to sell in its November 2026 report.

A growing market

The sale might be a record for the Riverland market, but Mr Kanizay hoped it signalled a change in thinking about regional properties.

"Five years ago, $1 million was a lot of money, and I think this should give people confidence," he said.

The house has a pool, a detached garage and an entertainment building. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"If you've invested in your home and you've made something special, back it in.

"You look at all the data metrics and everything out there, it says that regional SA is performing well."

The sale is the second highest in regional SA over the past year.

Ahead of it is a $6.25 million home on Hindmarsh Island, followed by a beachside Port Elliot property that sold for $4.5 million.

Back in the Riverland, a house in the nearby town of Paringa, branded the "transformer house", made national headlines after it was listed for $3.35 million in 2022.

The house has direct access to the River Murray. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

The price tag on that house was slashed to $2.65 million after sitting on the market for two years.

However, Mr Kanizay said the Renmark property was one of a kind.

"It's the best residential property I've sold in my 20-year career," he said.

title: Sydney buyer fears ending up 'on the streets' after deposits go missing
text:
Like hundreds of other impacted home buyers, Aziz Namazov and his family were excited to move into their newly built Landmark apartment in Sydney before their deposit vanished.

About three years ago, Mr Namazov and his wife bought an off-the-plan apartment in the Casa Delmar development in Dee Why.

"To do so, we had to sell our only property that we had," he said.

"We were meant to settle today [on the Dee Why unit]. A few days ago we received an email that settlement would not proceed, with no explanations.

" Then it became obvious that pretty much our deposits are now gone, and we don't know where. "

More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers have gone missing, with Landmark launching legal action against Branston Neville Lawyers and solicitor Ken Neville to recoup the missing funds.

More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers has gone missing. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

The developer alleges only part of the deposits held in trust were transferred to Hendrix Legal as directed after the company changed firms.

The matter is due to return to the Supreme Court on November 30.

The ABC has contacted Branston Neville Lawyers and Mr Neville for comment.

Almost 300 home buyers were due to get the keys to their newly built apartments between this week and early next year but have been left in limbo.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Dee Why development and about 145 purchasers at the Second Avenue development at Blacktown.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Casa Delmar development in Dee Why. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

The Landmark development in Blacktown remains under construction. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

Landmark founder Arash Tavakoli told the ABC: "Our purchasers are angry and frustrated, and they have every right to be.

" We are actively pursuing every avenue to get purchasers into their homes, including looking at whether they can move in before settlement. "

The Law Society of NSW confirmed it had suspended the practising certificate of Mr Neville and appointed a manager to Branston Neville Lawyers to "take control of the practice with immediate effect".

On Friday, a spokesperson said: "The Law Society is continuing its investigation, and further action is being considered."

Landmark projects missing unit deposits Almost 300 home buyers were waiting to get the keys to their newly built apartments in Sydney's Dee Why and Blacktown.

The Supreme Court of NSW made freezing orders, and subpoenas were issued to financial institutions to help establish where the funds were.

Mr Namazov and his family had been planning to move into their Dee Why apartment on December 2 and, in preparation, had terminated their lease on their current rental property.

They had also transferred their electricity, gas and internet plans over to the new property, with their belongings packed before they received the terrible news.

"We are facing a real, real chance that close to Christmas our family with two kids will be just out there on the streets with nowhere to go," he said.

Landmark says they are working to address the situation promptly. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

'Never thought this would happen'

Mr Namazov said the past few days had been "extremely stressful".

"My wife had a breakdown when she got the news … what we put in [our deposit] is two generations of hard work," he said.

'It's everything we have, that's our home."

Home buyers were due to get the keys to their units between this week and early next year. (ABC News)

Daniel Uzun de Oliveira is in the same predicament.

"We gave a deposit two years ago, that deposit was taken into a trust account … we have all the receipts and as far as we are aware, that money is gone," he said.

He and his family were supposed to settle last Wednesday, and move into their Dee Why unit on December 1.

Daniel Uzun de Oliveira is also impacted. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Mr Uzun de Oliveira had given his current rental property a termination notice in preparation for moving, and said he was thankful the landlord had since given them the all-clear to stay for now.

"Our solicitors are working and keeping us updated as much as they can," he said.

"It's stressful, it's frustrating. I came to Australia 11 years ago and never thought this would happen in a first world country."

'Why can't we settle?' says solicitor

Despite the Dee Why apartment complex being ready for buyers to move in, the legal action has left purchasers in limbo.

"The building is ready … we as buyers fulfilled our obligations in full, so we don't understand why we can't just settle in," Mr Namazov said.

Clare Wainwright is representing a number of buyers. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Wainwright Legal principal solicitor Clare Wainwright, who represents 42 affected Dee Why purchasers, said it was a distressing situation.

"It's honestly been some of the hardest news that we've had to communicate with them. In my entire career I've never had phone calls like this," she said.

"At the end of the day we've got purchasers without homes, there's already proceedings afoot that we're aware of in relation to those deposits … so why can't we settle? They [the buyers] have done all of the right things."

NSW Premier Chris Minns said the situation was "a concern".

"They [the deposits] should be held in trust accounts; if that hasn't been the case then there needs to be a full investigation," he said.

Chris Minns reacted to the missing deposits situation. (ABC News)

There were calls for the Law Society of NSW to lift the cap on the compensation available through its Fidelity Fund.

The fund is administered by the Law Society to compensate people who lose money due to law firms acting improperly in relation to trust funds or property.

It is capped at $1 million for claims relating to a single law practice, unless the Law Society authorises a greater payment. On Friday, a spokesperson said they would "consider whether to do so".

For now, the hundreds of buyers wait with bated breath.

"We are hoping for the best," Mr Namazov said.

title: Veggie workers allegedly underpaid and illegally hired in Gippsland
text:
Three vegetable farms around Bairnsdale in Victoria's east have been caught allegedly underpaying workers and using unlicensed labour hire companies.

Inspectors from the Victorian Labour Hire Authority (LHA) discovered the activity during unannounced visits in the region in recent weeks.

More than 20 workers on three farms were found to be employed through unlicensed labour hire providers.

They were picking and packing vegetables, including broccoli, green beans and lettuce.

During the inspections, LHA officers found records showing the workers were paid up to 35 per cent below the minimum horticulture rate.

Labour Hire Licensing Commissioner Wayne Gatt said it was a "significant concern".

"We know that workers at those locations are most vulnerable to exploitation," he said.

Wayne Gatt says farmers are responsible for checking if labour providers are registered. (Supplied: Labour Hire Authority)

Mr Gatt said the use of workers hired through unlicensed labour companies was illegal in Victoria.

"It's serious, to be quite honest," he said.

"People breaking the law face significant penalties in Victoria, up to $660,000 for a corporation.

"If you're an individual that's responsible for a company or responsible for the activity, up to $160,000."

Horticulture is a high-risk industry for worker exploitation due to the seasonal and transitory nature of the work and the high number of migrant workers.

More labour hire inspections are planned for other horticulture regions in Victoria. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

The LHA has stepped up inspections during the busy harvest period, with further visits planned in the Mildura, Yarra Valley and Shepparton areas.

"It's too late when inspectors are at your front gate to check if you're doing the right thing," Mr Gatt said.

At a time when 85 per cent of Australian vegetable growers are considering leaving the industry in the next 12 months because of high costs, according to peak body Aus Veg, Mr Gatt said compliance was even more important.

"If they're competing against people who aren't even paying their workers correct wages, that makes it even harder," he said.

"We know that growers are doing it tough, we know that the margins are tight, but the industry is not supported by people undercutting and acting unlawfully."

title: Company behind quashed Singleton Station water licence backs data centre plan
text:
A Central Australian cattle station at the centre of controversy over one of the nation's largest water licences has become the site of the latest proposal to establish a data centre in the Northern Territory.

Environmentalists have labelled the plan for Singleton Station, 130 kilometres south of Tennant Creek, "tone-deaf" and one they will fight "tooth and nail" due to a long-running dispute over a licence granted to owner Fortune Agribusiness to establish a 3,500 hectare irrigated fruit and vegetable farm at the site.

The Northern Territory government granted the company in 2021 the licence to extract 40 billion litres of water annually for 30 years, but native title holders fought the matter all the way to the High Court, which quashed the licence in August.

The decision to grant Singleton Station a water licence to extract 40 billion litres of water annually for 30 years was quashed in the High Court. (ABC News: Samantha Jonscher)

As the NT government reassesses Fortune Agribusiness's licence to irrigate the Singleton horticulture project, it has been revealed that the company has invested in Central Australia AI (CAAI) and a proposal to establish a hyperscale data centre on the station.

The Victorian-based CAAI did not respond to the ABC's request for an interview, but a LinkedIn post from its chair Russell Board says it is "developing a 1GW+ renewable-led AI and high-performance computing campus".

"The campus will have an integrated power supply comprising 3.3 GWp solar, 10GWh solar storage, 450 MW gas-backed reliability, a private HV grid, water-enabled cooling and strategic fibre in one master-planned platform," the post reads.

CAAI says it is developing a "AI and high-performance computing campus" at Singleton Station. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

An Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) extract shows Fortune Agribusiness holds 25 per cent of CAAI's shares. while a company that shares the same address and a similar name, Fortune AI, owns 37.5 per cent.

One of CAAI's four directors is well-known NT identity Vivian Oldfield, who bought Murranji cattle station, north of Elliott, in September last year.

Murranji Station is the planned home of Project Ares, another hyperscale data centre, which is currently undergoing an NT Environment Protection Authority environmental impact assessment.

In a statement, Fortune Agribusiness said the Singleton proposal was being discussed with the NT government and the Central Land Council (CLC), which represents Indigenous custodians across the Red Centre.

CLC general manager Josie Douglas said the land council was "notified very recently that there was a proposal for a data centre".

Josie Douglas says water use at the proposed data centre will likely be a concern for traditional owners. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

"It's in the very early stages of development and we expect to receive a full proposal from the company early next year," she said.

She said the CLC's role was "to represent the interests of native title holders and traditional owners, and we will be doing that once we receive a full proposal from the company".

She said she expected water for a data centre would be a concern for those "who have said from the very start water is precious", adding "we need water for the environment and water for country and water for people".

Protesters to fight 'tooth and nail' against proposal

Environmentalists have rejected the data centre plan, with a group of about 30 concerned citizens rallying outside NT Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne's electorate office in Alice Springs on Thursday morning.

The protesters decorated an office window with droplet-shaped cards featuring messages including "water is life" and "back off NT groundwater".

A group of protesters outside Joshua Burgoyne's office yesterday. (ABC News: Will Green)

The Arid Lands Environment Centre's Alex Vaughan labelled the data centre proposal as "shocking, outrageous, and tone-deaf".

"Communities across the NT and across this country are resisting AI data centres, but also we want to protect and conserve our groundwater, which is critical to our local economies, environments, cultures and communities," he said.

"It makes one of the largest groundwater grabs in the country even bigger and sees even more free water and more clearing of habitat.

" A super-campus AI data centre at Singleton Station will be resisted and we'll be fighting tooth and nail to make sure this proposal does not get up. "

Parliament passes new water laws

Mr Vaughan was also critical of the NT government's new water laws, which passed parliament on Thursday.

"The Northern Territory already has some of the weakest water laws in the country and these reforms are further gutting the Northern Territory's water laws," he said.

Alex Vaughan says the proposed data centre at Singleton Station is "outrageous". (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Ms Douglas agreed, saying the CLC was concerned that the government was assessing Fortune Agribusiness's water licence after the company had withdrawn its farm proposal from an environmental impact statement (EIS) evaluation.

"In terms of water planning in the NT, it's going backwards, and we have urged Mr Burgoyne not to make a decision on the water licence until he has had full consideration of the environmental impact assessment," she said.

"We would expect he would make a decision based on robust, sound evidence."

Protesters have criticised the CLP government's new water laws, which passed parliament this week. (ABC News: Will Green)

Fortune Agribusiness said in a statement it had withdrawn because it "considers it appropriate to await the minister's decision before progressing aspects of the EIS that may be affected by that decision".

"Our intention is to ensure the new EIS process can take account of the minister's decision and relevant new and updated scientific information," the statement said.

Mr Burgoyne said the current Fortune Agribusiness water licence under consideration was for the farm, and a data centre project would need separate approval.

title: Sam Walker signs with PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL season
text:
Premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has signed with the Papua New Guinea Chiefs for the 2028 season.

Walker, whose relationship with the Sydney Roosters fell apart after the club's grand final victory, will head to Port Moresby on a two-year deal.

The Queenslander is coming off the best year of his career, making State of Origin and Australian Test debuts.

"Sam is undoubtedly a gifted footballer who has already shown that he has tremendous vision, an outstanding kicking game and an ability to create something out of nothing," PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said.

"He is also a very smart footballer who understands how to influence and control a game and has shown that he can perform on the biggest of stages across club, state and now international level.

"We're really excited about what he can bring to the team and his partnership alongside Jarome Luai allows us to have one of the game's most creative and influential halves combinations — something which I'm excited to see develop as we take to the field."

Walker made his Test and Origin debuts this season. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The 24-year old was the 2021 Dally M Rookie of the Year and has been the Tricolours starter ever since.

He also attracted interest from South Sydney and Canterbury.

PNG Chiefs General Manager of Football Michael Chammas said the team believed Walker's best football was still yet to come.

"Sam was someone we identified as a player who we believe could have a transformational impact on our team — both in how we play on the field but also on the way we build our side and the way other players excel around him," Chammas said.

"He is a premiership winner, an Origin star and a World Cup winner and he has shown that he can perform under pressure in the biggest moments of our game.

Walker is the latest star signing for the PNG Chiefs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He is also still young and we believe that his best years are ahead of him.

"We're thrilled that Sam has committed to what we are building and we look forward to seeing him play a key role in the bright future of the PNG Chiefs."

Walker is the latest star signing for the Chiefs, who have created shockwaves in the player market with their ability to offer tax-free contracts.

In the past week, they have signed Canberra and New South Wales backrower Hudson Young and North Queensland star Jeremiah Nanai.

Luai, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and Joseph Manu will also line up for the Chiefs in their inaugural season.

Walker is the ninth player they have signed with either Test or Origin experience.

title: Victorian Coalition's election spending and saving explained
text:
On Thursday, just two days out from the state election, Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and the Coalition released their costed plans for spending and savings.

It was the first time Victorians got a proper glimpse of the Coalition's plan to rein in government spending if they win this Saturday's election.

Ms Wilson defended the decision to release the numbers so late in the campaign, after roughly 2 million Victorians had already voted, saying it was up to them when they decided to head to the ballot box.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) estimates the Coalition's policies will lower net debt by $20 billion over the next four years. You can read its full analysis here.

Here's how the Coalition plans to do it:

Assets sell-off

The Coalition has vowed to sell off or privatise a significant number of assets. This includes, but is not limited to:

Offering a 90-year lease of Melbourne Water's sewerage treatment business to a private operator.

Further privatising VicRoads, reducing the State's share from 19 per cent to 5 per cent.

Selling the Melbourne Market in Epping, which is the state's only wholesale fruit, vegetable and cut flower trading centre.

The sale of Delburn wind farm, and large-scale battery energy storage sites at Horsham and Plumpton.

Selling off land currently owned by Development Victoria, including in East Werribee, Cairnlea, Fisherman's Bend, Flora Hill and Mount Duneed, as well as the former Footscray Hospital Site and government-owned 565 Lonsdale Street.

Selling off the air rights above the Richmond station precinct.

These decisions have been costed by the PBO to save the budget $13.8 billion over the next four years.

Drawdown on contingencies

The Coalition plans to drawdown on available funds in the operating and asset contingencies in the budget each year. The costings state this will improve the budget's bottom line by $5.8 billion to 2029-30

TAC reinvestment

If it wins government, the opposition plans to reinvest money from the Transport Accident Commission (TAC) into road maintenance. This would save about $3.4 billion over forward estimates.

Government hiring freeze

It plans to introduce a hiring freeze across the 10 Victorian government departments until staff numbers return to 2014-2015 levels. The opposition says this will save $3.8 billion to 2029-30.

Kinder funding

The Coalition will cap Free Kinder for three and four-year-olds at 15 hours per week, after Labor promised to increase four-year-old kinder to 30 hours a week. It will also stop infrastructure funding for contracting new Victorian Government kindergarten at schools and early learning centres from January 2027. These measures have been costed to save $898.4 million to 2029-30.

Scrapping level crossing removal

Plans to upgrade level crossings on the Upfield line, as well ones in Yarraville and Spotswood, will be dumped under a Wilson government. It will also pause removals in Seaford until at least 2030. Breaking the contracts for this will cost $90 million, but ultimately it'll save the budget $2.1 billion.

Abolish the Victorian investment fund

The Coalition plans to abolish the Victorian Investment Fund, which provides grants to support business investment, innovation and economic growth, which the PBO costed as saving $61.1 million to 2029-30.

Pausing the Suburban Rail Loop

It's worth noting that the opposition plans to pause and review the Suburban Rail Loop project, meaning no contracts would be signed and new works will not be commenced during the period of review. The PBO says this review will have no impact on the budget's net position.

Budget spending

Pothole maintenance is one of the Liberals' key spending policies.

That's a wrap of some of the key budget savings, so now let's take a look and what the Coalition plans to spend money on, and the taxes it plans to cut:

Road maintenance

In one of its headline policies, the Coalition plans to invest $5 billion in road maintenance over the next four years, including eliminating a million potholes. It also wants to establish Better Roads Victoria, and boost roadside maintenance like slashing and drain clearance.

Road upgrades

Separately to the maintenance blitz, the opposition says it will also put $1.1 billion towards upgrading road infrastructure. This includes sections of roads in outer metropolitan areas, regional roads and freeways.

Scrapping emergency services tax

The Coalition plans to repeal the Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund (ESVF), and reinstate the Fire Services Property Levy (FSPL) from 1 July 2027. This decision will reduce the budget by $994.4 million over the next four years.

Abolish the AirBnb tax

The PBO believes the opposition's move to abolish the short-stay levy, otherwise known as the AirBnb tax, which applies to accommodation bookings of less than 28 days, will reduce the budget by $903.3 million to 2036–37.

Increasing stamp duty exemption

It also plans to increase the first home buyer stamp duty exemption to $1 million. This means any first home buyer who purchases a property below the value of $1 million will be exempt from the tax. This loss in revenue will be partially offset by the removal of the first home owner's grant. The PBO says this will take $781.4 million out of state coffers.

Regional trains

The Coalition plans to procure a fleet of 25 battery-electric trains to run on the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines by 2030-31. It also wants to increase regional services by repurposing 25 existing VLocity three-car trains from existing passenger rail services in Melbourne. This, along with network upgrades, was costed at $765.9 million over the next four years. The opposition has also promised $51.2 million to return rail passenger services to Mildura and Dimboola by mid-2029. However the PBO did not assess whether that funding would be sufficient to deliver the project.

School payroll tax

The Coalition says it'll roll back payroll tax on all non-government schools. In 2024 Labor introduced payroll tax on non-government schools with an income per student of above $15,000 a year. This will wipe $458.3 million from the budget over the next four years.

Country roads and bridges

A Wilson government would put $288 million towards a new 'Country Roads and Bridges' program, which would provide funding for rural and regional councils to upgrade local roads and bridges.

Weekly toll cap

Capping weekly spending on Victoria's toll roads at $50 per vehicle for individuals and small businesses, with a maximum toll cap rebate of $3,000 per year, will cost the budget bottom line $241.7 million to the year 2029-30. The Coalition, when announcing the plan, had said it would cost $180 million over the two years.

Fire services infrastructure investment

The opposition says it'll build new CFA stations and upgrade existing ones, as well as replace trucks, pumpers and tankers over the next five years. It also promises to increase funding for Fire Rescue Victoria. In total, this will cost the budget $240.1 million over the next four years.

New court of criminal appeal

It plans to establish a new and separate Court of Criminal Appeal in Victoria, costing $118.6 million to the year 2036–37. This would see criminal appeals be heard in the newly created court, instead of falling under the jurisdiction of Victoria's Court of Appeal, which rules on both criminal and civil cases.

title: Hobart stadium to proceed even without extra funds to cover cost increase
text:
The Tasmanian government says it will proceed with the Macquarie Point stadium even if it does not receive more funding from the Commonwealth or AFL in response to increasing cost estimates.

The government has also not set a maximum borrowing limit and has conceded that it has not kept its written commitment with an independent MLC to stick to its $875 million cap on the state's contribution.

The Macquarie Point Development Corporation found $100 million of "savings" during the design stage. (Supplied: MPDC)

The government's cost estimate for the stadium increased from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion, with the Commonwealth contributing $240 million to the broader precinct and the AFL adding $15 million.

The final cost rises to $1.54 billion once precinct and development costs are included.

Treasurer Eric Abetz and senior departmental staff answered questions at a parliamentary committee today, which included updates on negotiations with tenderers that are soon to conclude.

It was confirmed that the contract will be fixed price, rather than cost-plus.

Department of Premier and Cabinet secretary Kathrine Morgan-Wicks chairs a Macquarie Point stadium oversight committee, which also includes other departmental heads.

Kathrine Morgan-Wicks says "higher margins" were included in tender submissions than had been assumed previously. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

She told parliament that tenderers were seeking greater protection in the contract due to market risks, and that this had added to the cost estimate for the stadium.

"As market uncertainty has increased, impacted by the Iran war, tenderers are seeking greater protection against future cost escalation and project risk than was anticipated in earlier estimates," Ms Morgan-Wicks said.

"This has resulted in higher margins being included in tender submissions than had been assumed during previous planning phases."

Treasurer concedes commitment to cap taxpayer contributions will not be 'adhered to'

Prior to the final parliamentary vote on the stadium last year, Premier Jeremy Rockliff committed in writing to cap the state's contribution to $875 million.

Hobart's stadium and precinct costs rise to $1.54b The state government blames high oil, materials and labour prices for the blowout from a $1.13 billion budget set last year.

He wrote that if the estimate increased, the government would reduce the stadium's scope or seek further funds from the Commonwealth, AFL or Cricket Australia.

The stadium's developer — publicly owned Macquarie Point Development Corporation [MPDC] — had found $100 million of savings during the design stage.

The government has written to the other parties, as well as Cricket Tasmania, requesting additional funding, but did not confirm if it had received any responses.

Eric Abetz says he cannot provide a figure for how much the government would spend on the project. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Abetz said the funding cap would not be adhered to, citing the "unforeseen" Iran war.

"Are we able to abide by that commitment? At this stage, it doesn't look as though we can," he said.

Mr Abetz could not confirm how much the state was prepared to spend in total.

Dean Winter, Labor: How much over that cost cap is the government prepared to go? Mr Abetz: We will indicate all of that once we know what the final price is. Mr Winter: You've talked about seeking funding from [the Commonwealth, AFL, Cricket Australia]. In the event that they don't provide additional funding, will the government still proceed with the project? Mr Abetz: That would be my expectation, yes.

Not all funding sources yet clear

Cabinet will make its final decision on the stadium contract in the week leading up to December 18.

The Macquarie Point stadium oversight committee in front of the public accounts committee on Friday. (ABC News)

Murchison independent MLC Ruth Forrest questioned how MPDC could sign the contract if it did not have guaranteed funding.

Ms Forrest: We heard from the chair of MPDC … he indicated quite clearly he was unable to sign a contract without surety of the funding required, and obviously it's come in above what was agreed. If there's not hundreds of millions of dollars made available, how do you propose to give him the comfort to sign the contract? Mr Abetz: The board will need comfort, and that comfort will be provided through a facility from (public financing corporation) TasCORP.

Hobart's stadium price tag explained The cost to build Hobart's Macquarie Point stadium will rise by $100 million. But a swag of other expenses will add to the bill.

Ms Morgan-Wicks told the committee that overseas interest being shown in purchasing a 49 per cent stake in the Hobart Hurricanes Big Bash League club was promising for additional external investment in the stadium.

"Meetings that we've had with parties that are associated with that sale … we will be continuing to work through that over the coming months," she said.

The stadium's contingency figure has also not yet been determined; the previous contingency was an additional 14 per cent.

Bec Thomas believes 'cost cap' influenced process despite breach

Independent MLC Bec Thomas told ABC Radio Hobart that she stood by her decision to support the stadium in exchange for receiving written commitments from the premier, despite the cap no longer being adhered to.

Jeremy Rockliff committed in writing to cap the state's contribution to $875 million to gain support for the project from Bec Thomas. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

"It is clear that the cap of $875 million that I secured in order to support the stadium has influenced the behaviour of the Macquarie Point Development Corporation," she said.

"Without having that cap in place, we wouldn't probably be having these conversations.

"Ultimately, it's the government who is accountable for whether or not it sticks to its promises, isn't it?"

title: Mum welcomes 'horrifying' AI companion being removed from app store
text:
Controversial AI companion service Talkie is now blocking Australian and British visitors from its website, days after an ABC investigation prompted Apple to remove the product from its app store globally.

From this morning, Australian visitors to the site received a prompt saying Talkie was "currently not available in your region", while Talkie's listing in Apple's App Store remains absent.

The moves follow a joint investigation by the ABC and UK outlet The Bureau of Investigative Journalism into inappropriate and abusive interactions between Talkie's AI characters and children.

Companion AI apps like Talkie are popular among younger social-media users. (Supplied)

Talkie is one of the world's most popular AI companion apps, which allow users to talk through text and voice chats with a myriad of user-created fictional characters.

The investigation uncovered corporate documents showing its Chinese parent company, MiniMax, had engineered its AI models to create emotional bonds to keep users talking.

It also revealed evidence suggesting MiniMax was training its commercially-available AI models on Talkie user conversations, despite telling users they were "private".

MiniMax did not respond to questions about why it had begun geo-blocking Australian and British users.

App removal could affect financial outlook

Talkie was previously available on Apple and Google Android devices globally, and via the web.

Chinese research firm Unique Research this month estimated the app had 9.72 million active users per month, and 1.13 million average users on the web.

Now, analysts are warning the removal of Talkie's app could affect its financial outlook, amid a slump in the company's stock price.

Chinese AI app's abusive chats Parents around the world are sharing stories of inappropriate interactions between their children and a Chinese AI app called Talkie, alleging it manipulates users to train AI.

Apple removed the app from its global app store for breaking guidelines around sexual content after questions by the ABC.

Third-party app analytics platform AppInsider estimated Talkie had tens of thousands of daily downloads from the Apple app store.

This is consistent with a previous temporary removal of the Talkie app in 2024, which resulted in the loss of 16,800 daily downloads, according to MiniMax.

Talkie's Google Play listing shows it has been downloaded onto Android devices more than 50 million times, with data published by the Australian Competition & Consumer Commission (ACCC) showing this included 400,000 Australian downloads in the first half of 2024.

The app remains available on Google Play Store in Australia, but Google previously told the ABC its use was available only to verified adults.

A tough time for Chinese AI sector

Talkie's removal comes at an already difficult time for the Chinese AI industry, facing an industry-wide, months-long sell-off.

MiniMax, which owns Talkie through its Singaporean subsidiary SUBSUP, is down nearly 90 per cent from its peak six months ago.

The company's stock slumped a further 7 per cent since the release of the initial investigation, with analysts predicting the app's removal would put pressure on an important revenue source for the company.

Talkie and its Chinese sister app, Xingye, accounted for 63.7 per cent of MiniMax's revenue in 2024 and 35.1 per cent of the first nine months of 2025.

The app is also drawing the attention of Australian regulators.

Had an experience using an AI companion? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

In response to the ABC's investigation, Australian Information Commissioner Elizabeth Tydd referred to the incoming Children's Online Privacy Code, set to commence on December 10.

"It will be open for me to enforce the code through action including seeking the imposition of civil penalties up to $50 million per contravention," she said.

A spokesperson for the Office of the eSafety Commissioner said it was investigating Talkie, and has been talking to its operator.

"If the service returns, eSafety will continue to assess compliance with its obligations under the Online Safety Act."

Elizabeth Tydd says next month she will be able to enforce a new Children's Online Privacy Code. (ABC News: Josh Bavas)

'Really good start'

Brisbane mother Steph, who had spoken to the ABC and TBIJ about her 12-year-old daughter's "horrifying" interactions with Talkie, welcomed the decision to remove the app.

"Talkie being unavailable in Australia is a really good start. One down, thousands to go," she said.

Steph says banning Talkie is a good first step. (ABC News: Glen Armstrong)

Steph said she would like to see Australia pass a law restricting AI companion apps to adults, like with pornography and gambling.

She also called for "significant consequences" for apps that mislead users about their privacy or do not make it clear their data would be used to train AI models.

"These companies might be large, but they aren't untouchable. It's up to enough of us to stand up and say 'this is what we expect'," she said.

title: Lyon's career in limbo as he faces Test axe
text:
Nathan Lyon is set to be axed from Australia's squad for the first Test in a move that raises questions over the 39-year-old's future in the team.

Australia will on Saturday name their squad for the December 9 series opener against New Zealand in Perth, but it is understood Lyon will not be included.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner when fit for more than 13 years, but selectors have shown a willingness to go without a specialist tweaker more often recently.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

He has three times been left out of Australia's team over the past 18 months, with selectors picking four quicks in Tests against West Indies, England and South Africa.

But the spinner's omission from the squad is even more notable, given previous such calls have been made on seeing the final wicket closer to the toss.

Lyon has made no secret of his desire to continue playing, with legacy-defining tours of India and England in the next nine months.

The sixth-leading wicket-taker of all time with 577 scalps, Lyon worked around the clock to recover from a hamstring injury last summer and return to the Test side.

His push has included giving up alcohol and spending more time in the gym, having previously described how he is trying to squeeze every last bit out of his career, with 145 Tests already to his name.

Nathan Lyon struggled to make a breakthrough in the latter stages of the third Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

Where that career goes from here is now in question.

Lyon took six wickets at 43.67 in Australia's most recent tour of South Africa, where he was overlooked for Scott Boland in a wet second Test in Gqeberha.

Included in that was Australia's inability to take wickets on the fourth day of the final Test in Cape Town, as South Africa recovered from a 100-run first-innings deficit.

South Africa spinner Simon Harmer then bagged 6-16 on the final day to bowl the Proteas to victory.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

Lyon has since taken seven Sheffield Shield wickets across two matches on return to Australia, but was out-bowled by Queensland leg spinner Mitchell Swepson in Sydney this week.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald had indicated after the loss in Cape Town that Lyon remained Australia's number one spinner, when asked if that would be reviewed.

"Review it?" McDonald responded at the time.

"I don't think it's something to review now. We'll sit back and we'll go through Shield cricket.

"Nathan will be preparing for the first Test match in Perth."

A decade ago, before quitting to focus on his golf career, Nicolai von Dellingshausen was on track to become a pilot with Lufthansa. Though he didn’t get his wings, the unheralded German is still flying high after carding an eight-under par second round 64 to go with his opening 67 to lead by three shots at the halfway mark of the Australian PGA Championship. The same couldn’t be said of Australian star Lucas Herbert, whose hopes of a maiden Australian PGA crown quickly nosedived on Friday afternoon after the 30-year-old, who finished tied-sixth in this year’s Open Championship at Royal Birkdale, had horror round of 77 to miss the cut. Germany’s Nicolai Von Dellingshausen is the halfway leader. Getty Images The news was better for compatriot and fellow former LIV defector Cameron Smith, who rocketed into contention by carding 64 to move into outright third at nine-under. Tournament favourite Adam Scott battled to get going in the blustery afternoon conditions, but managed to make the cut despite some struggles after the turn to be two-under. And there was jubilation for Camden Golf Club pro Robbie Minns, who wowed the crowd late on Friday with a hole-in-one on the 18th to win a BMW X5 worth more than $150,000.

“I’m still in shock,” Minns – whose official world ranking is 5002 –said. “I hit a decent shot, it was a little bit heavy ... I’ve looked down, and I see everyone going off – and it’s gone in the hole.” Von Dellingshausen’s round was headlined by a spectacular albatross on the par-four 14th at The Lakes Golf Course in Sydney, as the 33-year-old went to the clubhouse as the soaraway outright leader at 13-under. Loading The world No.333 leads rising Northern Irishman Tom McKibbin, who carded a seven-under to sit three shots back at -10. The 23-year-old is mentored by Rory McIlroy, having played at the same Holywood Gold Club, and will join the double Masters champion in Melbourne for the Australian Open next week at Kingston Heath. Sitting one place further back in third is Smith. The 33-year-old has not won in three years but roared back to form on Friday and will go into the weekend firmly in contention to claim his fourth Australian PGA championship.

With storms expected on Saturday afternoon, the third round will start an hour earlier and Smith will tee off alongside the overseas pair in a three-ball. Smith was one of two Australians to finish inside the top 10 after 36 holes, with Cam Davis sitting tied-eighth after carding a one-under to head into the weekend at six-under. Cameron Smith showed signs that he was getting back to his best at the Australian PGA. Getty Images Round-one leader and world No.560 Haydn Barron failed to back up his stellar 64 on Thursday, but is still in the mix alongside fellow Aussie Travis Smyth, who carded a four-under. Championship drawcard Min Woo Lee endured an up-and-down day to finish at three-under after 36 holes. While Smith set the pace early, von Dellingshausen stole the show and made use of the friendlier morning conditions.

The German started his round with a birdie on the first and was four-under through 13, before stunning the gallery by holing out with his second shot on the par-five 14th. title: Implosion: The downfall of China’s money king
text:

The gala in Xiong’an was meant to be an extravagant affair. The host, CreditEase, a rare Chinese wealth manager with a stellar reputation, was turning 20. Its founder, Tang Ning, wanted to show his appreciation for the Communist Party, whose boss, Xi Jinping, handpicked Xiong’an as a big city-building project. The date was set for late May. Then the event was abruptly cancelled. CreditEase collapsed soon after. In October, Tang, his wife and many of his employees were detained. Earlier this month his firm’s 11-year-old New York-listed unit said it faced delisting.

The fiasco has shaken China’s investment industry. CreditEase was as trusted as such firms get in Chinese finance. It now owes some 100,000 clients $US4.4 billion ($6.6 billion) in principal. Its troubles add to a long list of implosions causing financial insecurity for millions of Chinese.

CreditEase chief Tang Ning, his wife and many of his employees were detained in October. AP

Founded in 2006, CreditEase was a pioneer of peer-to-peer (P2P) lending. It connected wealthy folk with cash to spare to others in need of it and willing to pay high interest rates, circumventing clunky state banks and helping discover true market prices for credit. Tang spawned thousands of imitators. Many lent to risky borrowers eschewed by banks. Some absconded with investors’ cash. In 2016 the state began tightening previously lax rules, and by 2020 most forms of P2P were banned. The majority of providers either collapsed or were wound down. Many bosses were detained.

Tang found a way to keep CreditEase going. The firm lent money to borrowers and then passed bundles of loans to intermediaries, which in turn packaged them into fixed-income products listed on provincial or municipal asset exchanges. These products’ guaranteed yield of 8 per cent over one to three years, making them popular with investors whose money made its way back to CreditEase. The firm then used the proceeds to make more loans. Passing through a public exchange legitimised the process. Tang’s links to officials in Beijing probably helped, too, says an insider.

One of modern football’s most successful partnerships has fractured, with Collingwood parting ways with list boss Justin Leppitsch following ongoing tensions with premiership coach Craig McRae. The Magpies confirmed Leppitsch’s immediate departure on Friday afternoon, bringing an abrupt end to a five-season tenure that helped deliver one of the most remarkable transformations in the club’s history. Magpies coach Craig McRae speaks with assistant Justin Leppitsch during the club’s 2023 premiership year. Getty Images The professional relationship between McRae and Leppitsch, forged when they were teammates in Brisbane’s era of supremacy at the turn of the century and then rekindled during Richmond’s premiership dynasty, was central to Collingwood’s renaissance. But the relationship that underpinned so much of Collingwood’s success has become increasingly strained, with Leppitsch’s departure the subject of speculation in senior football circles for some time.

Advertisement

Justin Leppitsch is on the move from Collingwood. AFL Photos The irony of Leppitsch’s exit is that two men who helped engineer Collingwood’s ascent to the summit of Australian football will no longer work together as the club confronts the complexities of sustaining that success. The timing of his departure is particularly significant given Collingwood finds itself at a delicate juncture in its list evolution, attempting to reconcile its immediate premiership ambitions with the inevitable generational change confronting its ageing playing group. In the short term, football general manager Charlie Gardiner will assume responsibility for list management while the Magpies determine the future structure of their football department. The relationship between a senior coach and a list manager is among the most consequential in any football club, particularly when the competing demands of immediate success and long-term sustainability become increasingly difficult to reconcile.

Advertisement

Collingwood’s unsuccessful pursuit of Richmond premiership defender Jayden Short during this year’s trade period came amid speculation about the relationship between McRae and Leppitsch. There was also scrutiny of Leppitsch’s public commentary surrounding the future of premiership midfielder Jordan De Goey, who comes out of contract at the end of next season. Craig McRae and Justin Leppitsch teamed up at Collingwood in the 2020s (main), Brisbane in the 2000s, with Michael Voss (top right) and at Richmond in the 2010s (bottom right). Getty Leppitsch subsequently confirmed during the trade period that both De Goey and rebounding defender Dan Houston would remain at Collingwood in 2027. The acquisitions of dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman medallist Jesse Hogan in October were the clearest indication yet that the Magpies believe their premiership window remains open.

Advertisement

Neither acquisition required Collingwood to sacrifice significant draft capital, allowing the club to supplement its existing group with established talent while retaining some capacity to invest in the next generation. Related Article AFL 2027 Suspended Swans return for AFL pre-season; Essendon build ruck depth at rookie draft On trade deadline night in October, Leppitsch talked of Collingwood’s controversial strategy of never wanting to allow their list to bottom out. “As a club, and [chief executive officer] Craig Kelly’s driven this, we don’t want empty stands. We want to give ourselves the ability to win consistently while nabbing a flag along the journey, as opposed to the longer path, which we all know what that is,” he said. “There might come a day where we have to do that … but we don’t feel like it’s in the near future.”

Advertisement

Whoever succeeds Leppitsch will inherit one of the more intriguing list management assignments in the competition: overseeing the transition away from some of the most accomplished players in Collingwood’s history while constructing a team capable of capitalising on the prime years of superstar midfielder Nick Daicos. Leppitsch initially joined the Magpies as an assistant coach ahead of the 2022 season before moving into strategy and innovation and eventually assuming responsibility for list management following the departure of former football boss Graham Wright. Wright, now chief executive of Carlton, was another of the central architects of Collingwood’s 2023 premiership. The Magpies have undergone considerable change in their football department since defeating Brisbane in that grand final, with Leppitsch the latest of the influential figures behind that triumph to depart the club.

Advertisement

“The 2023 premiership was no doubt a highlight, but I’d like to particularly thank our current list management and recruiting team – it has been a privilege to work alongside such talented and dedicated people,” Leppitsch said. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 No second chance: Why Buckley and Simpson were overlooked Leppitsch, who played in three consecutive premierships alongside McRae at Brisbane under Leigh Matthews, has accumulated considerable experience across almost every facet of a football department since his retirement as a player. He spent three seasons as senior coach of the Lions between 2014 and 2016 before returning to Richmond, where he was part of Damien Hardwick’s coaching team during the Tigers’ era of premiership dominance from 2017-20. His reunion with McRae at Collingwood in late 2021 represented the continuation of a professional association that spanned more than two decades.

Together, they helped transform a club that had finished second-last in 2021 into a preliminary finalist the following year and a premiership team the year after that. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. Sign up for the Real Footy newsletter.

In mid-October Will Cowper stood in the middle of Pici and surveyed his first restaurant as co-owner. It was very much a construction site. It was dirt floors and exposed framing and random equipment and all sorts of other gubbins strewn about the place. Downstairs, an earthmover sat silent behind a high-vis barrier mesh. Pici opens next week, Wednesday, December 2. Markus Ravik Five weeks later, Cowper sits in Pici and looks you dead in the eye, his ready smile dropping for a moment. “The last three weeks have probably been the hardest of my life. It’s been really difficult,” he says. “Now, it just feels surreal.”

Advertisement

Surreal because it’s over. Pici is finished. And it’s hard to believe it ever looked like a construction site, such is its sense of presence. It’s a real looker – absolutely a contender for the prettiest of the year. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article One of 2026’s best openings is from two chefs you’ve never heard of Cowper is opening the restaurant with his wife, pastry chef Gianna Cowper, and Andrew and Andrea Solomon, best known as co-operators of The Fish Factory. Cowper’s done this before. He opened Otto Brisbane – a restaurant he will long be associated with – at 480 Queen in 2016, and then moved with it to South Bank in 2021. “480 was similar because you’re coming up from Sydney, building a team from scratch,” he says. “But this has been a thought process about where things are, where things need to be. How are we going to do everything? How do we build the team? It’s a million little things.” Alkot Studio was in charge of the design. They’ve helped produce one of prettiest openings of the year. Matt Shea

Advertisement

The delay was caused by issues with some of the heritage aspects of the building. But the upshot was that once the green light reappeared, much of the build was ready to simply slot into place. It’s a venue of bold marble and rich dark timber and exposed brick and mirrored surfaces. Designers Alkot Studio have left the general layout similar to Gerties before it, with the bar up top and the dining space half a floor down on the Brunswick Street side. But then you remember that the Cowpers and Solomons knocked down the wall to what was Hellhound, giving Pici much more space. Pici’s kitchen sits on the lower floor that used to be shared by Gerties and Hellbound next door. Markus Ravik The open low-countered kitchen is on this floor, parked up against the back wall. Its eye-catching feature is a fairly hefty woodfire grill custom-made for Cowper by Sydney’s Platinum Commercial Kitchens. Pici’s menu will, as is standard nowadays, change with the seasons. Similar to Otto – and many a modern Australian Italian restaurant – it’s split into snacks, entrees, pastas and mains, but that’s where the similarity to Otto ends. No one would argue an on-form Otto is poor value, given the experience, but you wouldn’t say it’s cheap either.

Advertisement

Pici, on the other hand, is keenly priced. None of the entrees are more than $30, and most of the pastas hover about the $40 mark. It’s designed to encourage return visits from the locals. But it should also mean, very simply, that more people will now get to experience Cowper’s cooking, which is a nice thought. Champagne lobster ravioli with semi dried tomato ‘acqua pazza’ and basil. text:

LifestyleLife & relationshipsAir travel Qantas bosses won’t be pleased, but I just found the key to national unity Inside the departure lounge, we should all spare a thought for the people going nowhere. Sophie Quick November 27, 2026 — 5:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve just come back from a week away on holiday and I’ve realised that, unfortunately, when I’m at an airport, I can’t completely recognise the full humanity of other people. I am the Main Character, containing multitudes, and everyone I encounter is either an angel or an antagonist depending on whether they are helping or hindering me as I navigate the terminal. Angel: the security guy pointing out the sunglasses I almost left on the x-ray tray. Antagonist: the high-heeled lady with her portable scales, fat-shaming my suitcase at the departure gate. Angel: the woman who shifted her seat so we could both use a phone-charging port in the food court. Antagonist: child watching Paw Patrol at full volume. For everyone else, I feel nothing at all. It’s all about me – my needs, my departure time – until I have reached my destination, when I can (hopefully) snap back into regular form. Photo: Robin Cowcher I don’t think I’m the only one who feels this chilling effect at the airport. There are a few obvious reasons for it. You have to focus in the terminal because you’ll lose a lot of money if you miss your flight. The atmosphere of biometric surveillance – where every person is reduced to scannable data – is surely part of it too. Proximity to Qantas employees causes knock-on morale issues. (This is a shame. Hostility towards the executive leadership team running our national carrier should energise and unite all non-Qantas executive Australians! Sadly it just makes most of us tired.)

Advertisement

On screen, depictions of airports veer towards extremes. On one hand, airport terminals are sometimes treated as homogenous, transient “non-places”. (I’m thinking, especially, of the George Clooney movie Up in the Air). Or they’re places of high emotion and high stakes (from Home Alone, Love Actually and Carry On to reality TV shows like Border Security). My own experience tends more towards the first version, and I think that’s because I have not (yet) presented to an airport with humanitarian needs, access requests, urgent romantic confessions or smuggling objectives. Related Article Allergies Bless me (sniff), for I have endured the season of sinus congestion The modern airport experience is catered to people like me: able-bodied, digitally literate and English-speaking. Airlines would like to discourage human needs and human complications because they don’t want to pay human beings to deal with those things. I think their bad faith is rubbing off on me. Perhaps I should take inspiration from on-screen airport workers. Earlier this year, I binged the SBS hit series The Airport Chaplain (starring Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez). I’m now watching the 2024 comedy series How Not To Die Alone, set in JFK Airport (starring Natasha Rothwell). The first of these – about a chaplain who provides “emotional, spiritual and practical support” for passengers passing through the fictional Victoria Airport – falls firmly in the camp of high-stakes, high-emotion airport drama. How Not to Die Alone is more of a workplace comedy. They are both great series that dramatise complex workplace dynamics. And they’re both good reminders that while I – and many other passengers – may act like robots during our transient airport hours, there’s a lot going on for others, including the people who work there every day. Many airport jobs are, of course, highly exposed to economic instability and automation.

Advertisement

There’s a lot going on behind closed doors, too. My favourite thing about both these shows – and even about Border Security – is the scenes showing the bizarre variety of seized and surrendered goods in the restricted zone. In The Airport Chaplain there’s a storyline, based on a true story from Melbourne Airport, where a passenger tries to pass through security with live exotic fish hidden in plastic bags strapped to her legs. In How Not to Die Alone, Mel and her friend go looking in the surrendered items department for prescription painkillers and discover a $4000 luxury ham. In real life, I’m very grateful to the people who stop dangerous stuff getting onto planes or through customs. I’m glad they do what they do. But on a less practical level, it’s nice to reflect on how weird and unpredictable people are – especially in the dehumanising environment of the airport. In the departure hall, it’s all touchscreen kiosks and WHSmith. But the restricted security zone is a world of mystery fluids, experimental dairy products and confiscated frogs. It’s a world of bonkers human fetish and conspiracy. I’ll try to keep that in mind next time I enter an airport terminal and feel myself slipping into Main Character mode. It’s not just me who contains multitudes. Other passengers contain multitudes (of tropical fish in their pants, possibly) and I might be standing next to one of them.

title: What happens when you privatise poo? Victoria could be about to find out
text:
In brief Experts say Jess Wilson's plan to sell management of Melbourne sewerage while maintaining public ownership is still privatisation.

One Nation, the Greens and Labor have all criticised the plan.

Two days before the Victorian election, state Opposition leader Jess Wilson unveiled a debt-reduction plan centred on the privatisation of swathes of land, renewable energy assets, air rights — and the leasing of the state's sewage treatment facilities.

The Coalition says a one-off $9.2 billion payment from a 90-year lease on Melbourne's sewerage would help fund a promised $20 billion reduction in net debt by 2030.

For close to a century, the Coalition will lease the Western Treatment Plant in Werribee, the Eastern Treatment Plant in Bangholme, nine pumping stations and 400km of sewerage beneath our streets.

The decision has drawn backlash from environmental groups and political parties, including the Greens and Labor, which earlier this year was revealed to have abandoned pursuit of a similar idea led by former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan.

Professor Monzur Imteaz, an environmental engineering expert at Swinburne University, said transferring operation of Melbourne's two largest sewage facilities to commercial operators could deliver prompt, dependable service for two reasons: because private firms "usually" escape the red tape that slows public agencies, and because fresh capital could fund modern, higher-performing technology.

However, he told SBS News: "Upgraded infrastructure carries a price, and households would probably shoulder it through higher charges."

Imteaz said the Opposition is yet to explain how it would "restrain those escalations".

READ MORE The election surprise One Nation didn’t see coming

On Thursday, Wilson said the Essential Services Commission would continue to regulate water prices following the lease.

But Munirul Nabin, a senior lecturer in economics at Deakin University, said the arrangement warranted serious consideration.

"In economic terms, the Coalition is proposing giving operational control to a profit-motivated private company, under government price regulation," Nabin told SBS News.

"A private operator will always have a profit motive. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but if the government also caps prices, it can create distortions."

If a private company has exclusive operating rights for 90 years, it effectively becomes a monopoly operator, he said, adding that "the issue isn't ownership", but "who holds the power".

And if something were to go wrong, such as a natural disaster or drought, the private operator would have significant renegotiating power.

"People are already struggling with rising living costs and higher utility bills, and if a profit-motivated operator takes over, I believe prices will eventually increase one way or another."

Is a 90-year lease privatisation?

The Coalition took plans to privatise Melbourne Water to the 2018 and 2022 elections, but Wilson ruled it out earlier this year.

"We're not touching it," she told ABC News.

On Thursday, she argued the proposal was not privatisation because ownership would remain with the state.

"We're not privatising Melbourne Water. What we are doing is offering a 90-year lease for the sewerage assets to bring the interest bill down in this state."

Graeme Hodge, a privatisation and regulation expert and emeritus professor of law at Monash University, said this distinction was "nonsense".

"Calling a 90-year lease 'not privatisation' is, in my view, nonsense. That's political gameplay," he told SBS News.

"If you hand over the use of assets for 90 years, or 99 years as they do in places like Hong Kong and Saudi Arabia, then of course it's a privatisation."

Nabin agreed that in economic terms, "handing over operational control for three generations is functionally similar to privatisation", and warned the model created tensions between profit incentives and price regulation.

"Reducing debt is important, but any plan needs to address both the short- and long-term consequences," he said, adding that the policy was short-sighted.

Environmental concerns

The Victorian Greens and Labor have pointed to the United Kingdom as an example of the potential consequences of privatising water management.

Britain privatised its water sector in 1989. Since then, household bills have risen faster than inflation and regulators have faced criticism over sewage pollution.

In 2022, the UK's Environmental Audit Committee warned in a submission to an inquiry into river health that water companies appeared to be dumping untreated or partially treated sewage in rivers regularly, and that the impact of wastewater from sewage treatment works and sewer overflows was preventing 36 per cent of water bodies from achieving good ecological status.

"What we learned from the UK is that it wasn't a very good privatisation. They didn't put sufficiently strong regulation in place to control the private companies involved, and people received poorer services as a result," Hodge said.

"Even now, decades later, they're still trying to get the balance right."

Environmental groups have expressed concern that the lease risks disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including internationally important wetlands that support migratory birds from across the globe.

Professor Richard Kingsford, a Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert, said the Western Treatment Plant was one of Australia's most important sites for waterbirds.

"Melbourne Water carefully manages nutrient levels in treated sewage to protect the health of Port Phillip Bay," he said.

"Maintaining these internationally important wetlands requires considerable ecological expertise, ongoing investment and careful management, which is hard to reconcile with companies whose objective is profit."

Hodge said that while privatisation could "make a lot of sense" if assets are run poorly, are run down, or managed incompetently, "that's not Victoria's situation".

"Victoria has one of the cleanest water supplies in the world through Melbourne Water and an excellent sewage treatment system.

"So I'm disappointed that politicians feel the need to privatise it."

While it was "impossible to say" whether privatisation arrangements always fail or always succeed, "the biggest winners from privatisation are, firstly, governments that receive the cash, and secondly, investors, who on average do very well", Hodge said.

"Private investors are not stupid — they acquire assets at what they regard as a good price and work them hard to make profits for their shareholders."

On Friday, One Nation said it would not support the plan, with Victorian leader Warren Pickering saying it was "privatisation in all but name".

title: David Shoebridge says the Greens need to stop 'preaching'. He's also not ruling out UFOs
text:
Key Points: David Shoebridge is predicting a Victorian Greens surge while arguing One Nation lacks a clear agenda.

The Greens leader has framed inequality and wealth redistribution as central to the Greens' mission.

Greens leader David Shoebridge says one of his party’s biggest problems has been spending too much time telling voters what it thinks rather than listening to what they want.

In a wide-ranging interview with SBS News as federal parliament wrapped for the year on Friday, Shoebridge reflected on the future of the Greens, wealth inequality, the Victorian election, sanctions against Russia and even unidentified aerial phenomena.

Shoebridge became the Greens' sixth leader on 30 September in a rare contested ballot after Larissa Waters resigned due to ill health. He then declared the party was "here to replace" Labor, and "beat down One Nation" by filling what he described as a Labor "policy vacuum" to build a "progressive, positive mass movement".

Despite his rhetoric, the Greens negotiated deals with the Albanese government this week to pass online safety laws, increase taxes on trusts, and retain pensioners' private health insurance rebates, in exchange for concessions including bigger fines for tech companies and higher private jet fuel taxes.

Shoebridge said the Greens need to "do a better job of connecting with people who are under pressure".
