Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"[We need to be] listening to people struggling with rent, mortgages, power bills and the cost of food," Shoebridge told SBS News.

"Not preaching solutions at them."

'The 99 per cent' versus the 1 per cent

Shoebridge said addressing inequality is central to the Greens' policies.

"We can see that there’s increasing concentrations of wealth in the 1 per cent or a fraction of the 1 per cent and how the rest of society is being pretty much sold out on an almost routine basis by key decision-makers, not least the federal parliament," he said.

"We're not here to tell people why billionaires and multinational corporations must continue getting richer.

"We're here to shift wealth away from billionaires and into the pockets of Australians who need it for food, power bills and housing."

Shoebridge described discretionary trusts as "basically a rort for the ultra-wealthy" and "only a tiny fraction of small businesses" use them. However, business groups warn these changes will impose substantial restructuring costs on thousands of small and family businesses.

According to accountancy body CPA Australia, the compliance costs for families and businesses affected by the discretionary trust changes are between $2 billion and $3 billion for advice, plus $220 million to $600 million per year in ongoing costs.

Shoebridge said people with enormous wealth can effectively buy political influence; it's dangerous for democracy and the economy.

"When you base your politics on fundamental truths like that, people recognise it," he said.

"In some ways it's like saying the emperor has no clothes. People are relieved that somebody is finally talking about it."

A Victorian test against One Nation

The Greens' electoral strategy is to offer voters angry with the major parties a left-wing alternative to One Nation, which he believes offers "meanness, nastiness and having a go at your neighbour".

"This idea of a One Nation surge seems to have collided with reality, where people are trying to work out what One Nation actually stands for," he said.

Polling from the final Victorian Newspoll and Demos AU polls indicated support for One Nation had dropped to 16-18 per cent, down from 25 per cent in Wednesday's Resolve poll. However, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson received passionate and broad support in Victoria at several campaign events on Friday, on the eve of the state election.

The Greens leader said promises of cheaper groceries through publicly owned stores, free public transport and making wealthy people and companies "pay their fair share” led him to a confident prediction of a "Green surge" in the state election.

READ MORE The election surprise One Nation didn’t see coming

In the run-up to the state election, polling suggests the Greens may gain lower-house seats while One Nation will struggle to turn its support into strong results. One recent poll put both parties on 16 per cent of the primary vote; modelling suggests the Greens could gain two or three lower-house seats.

"For the first time, in what's becoming a four-way contest, voters are taking a serious look at what the Greens are offering," he said.

Sanctions: 'Messaging' without substance

Shoebridge also took aim at the government over sanctions enforcement.

An audit of Australia’s sanctions system by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO), released on Wednesday, found about 80 per cent of the actions taken involved nothing more than warning letters.

The government has accepted the audit's recommendations and is working to strengthen enforcement.

"What the ANAO report shows is that we have a Labor government that’s all about messaging, and not about substance," Shoebridge said.

Shoebridge has repeatedly opposed Australia sending weapons or military aid to Ukraine unless it is authorised by the United Nations Security Council while backing humanitarian, financial, and civilian assistance as well as tougher sanctions on Russian oil.

Opposing sending weapons to Ukraine without a United Nations mandate has caused dozens of Greens members to quit the party, given Russia has a permanent seat and veto power on the UN Security Council, the Australian Financial Review reported on Friday.

When asked if the audit showing sanctions are not being enforced changes his view, Shoebridge said one of the best ways we can support the people of Ukraine is through significant humanitarian and civilian assistance.

"At the same time, we should cut off the flow of money to the Russian military," he said. "Roughly 40 per cent of Russia's budget comes from oil revenue, and this government refuses to close loopholes that allow Russian oil to be refined through third countries and then imported into Australia."

An open mind on UFOs

Former Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson asked questions in Senate Estimates and other parliamentary forums about unidentified aerial phenomena, which have been under investigation by United States government agencies and others for more than 80 years.

Shoebridge said he used to say to Whish-Wilson that "as long as they're unidentified, they're in his portfolio".

"If they start making contact and they're friendly, then they'd move into foreign affairs," he said. "If they turn out to be hostile, we'd probably shift them into defence.

"So I think we're still at the first stage. Look at the evidence. Keep an open mind. There are lots of reports and witness accounts. Some of that evidence could support a number of different conclusions. At this stage, I simply have an open mind. I think it's foolish to look at the available information and declare with certainty that it's definitely one thing or another."

title: China's top officials are falling. Here's how the purge has unfolded
text:
IN BRIEF An investigation into Shanghai secretary Chen Jining is "particularly shocking", an analyst says.

It is part of sweeping expulsions in China's top brass.

Chinese President Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption campaign has claimed some of the country's most powerful political and military figures, reshaping the leadership ranks of the Communist Party and removing officials once considered untouchable.

Supporters say the drive has strengthened party discipline and public trust, while critics argue it has also helped Xi consolidate power ahead of a key party congress expected in 2027.

The campaign escalated again this week when China's anti-corruption watchdog announced an investigation into Politburo member and Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining, one of the country's most senior civilian officials.

Chen, 62, is accused of "suspected severe violations of discipline and laws", a phrase commonly used by Chinese authorities to refer to corruption and other political offences.

The investigation follows the purge of three other members of the elite leadership body, which was formed in 2022 with 24 members.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Now, with Chen under investigation, there are 21 acting members — China's Central Military Commission (CMC) vice chair Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the body last month.

Chen, a UK-educated environmental scientist, was appointed environmental protection minister in 2015, before becoming Beijing's mayor. In 2022, he joined the Politburo in the party's chief position in Shanghai.

The position is part of a well-trodden path to the party's top leadership post — once being held by both current President Xi Jinping and former president Jiang Zemin.

Wen-Ti Sung, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub, told the Reuters news agency Chen's investigation is "particularly shocking".

"Chen's purge is particularly shocking in that he poses no military threat, and doesn't deviate from Xi on major symbolic issues like ethnic policy," Sung said, referring to Xi's emphasis on integration into mainstream Chinese culture.

"But he got purged anyway, so far without even an explanation. The shock is bound to reverberate."

Chen Jining, Party Secretary of Shanghai and member of Politburo, is being investigated for corruption. Source: AFP / Adek Berry

China expert Jean ⁠Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich said Chen's probe "sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the Party’s 'self-revolution'".

"If anything, it continues to intensify," he told Reuters.

Millions of CCP members and officials have been caught up in Xi's anti-graft campaign that has now been running for 14 years.

Recently, a record 33 dignitaries were expelled when the CCP's powerful Central Committee gathered. It came as the 21st Party Congress was for the second half of 2027 , effectively starting proceedings for China's tightly choreographed, twice-a-decade top reshuffle, when Xi is expected to extend his rule for another five-year term.

The party's fifth plenum saw leaders place political loyalty front and centre, as they vowed to keep purging 'impurities and viruses' from party ranks ahead of next year's congress.

Xi is "clearing the ground" before next year's gathering, sweeping aside entrenched political customs and older networks to build a more ideologically aligned leadership lineup, a senior Asian diplomat said.

The Central Committee, "with comrade Xi Jinping at its core", has "eliminated serious hidden dangers within the party, the state and the military," Zhang Fuhai, deputy secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, said on Friday.

The party, he told reporters at a news briefing, had been guided by the sense of mission that "we would rather offend thousands than let down 1.4 billion people", referring to China's population.

Three major officials expelled

Chen is the fourth Politburo member investigated in just over a year as the anti-corruption drive reaches the CCP's innermost circle, having already ensnared Central Military Commission vice chairmen Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.

Ma left his post as Xinjiang party chief in July 2025 and has been absent from public view since appearing at a major party meeting in October last year.

His investigation was publicly announced in April. He was accused of "serious violations of law and discipline" and expelled from the party in July — weeks after his dismissal from the National People's Congress.

Ma Xingrui was indicted on bribery charges in November. Source: AFP / Greg Baker

Ma was accused of large-scale "family corruption" and seeking benefits from others in the appointment of officials and improper job arrangements. The country's anti-corruption watchdog said he helped relatives purchase property at below-market prices and engaged in exchanges involving power and money for sex.

In November, China's top prosecuting agency indicted Ma on bribery charges.

Ma began his career in regional politics in the affluent southern province of Guangdong.

He had also served at the China National Space Administration and was vice minister of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

Zhang was placed under probe in January and then removed from the CMC in August.

The former first-ranked vice-chairman of the CMC was accused of disloyalty to the party and of abandoning party principles, as well as of corrupt self-enrichment and abuse of office.

Analysts said the corruption charges were not unusual, but the allegations of disloyalty, including forming cliques and factions, were unusually explicit.

Zhang was one of the few leading officers with combat experience, whose father had fought in the civil war alongside Xi's father.

China's Central Military Commission Vice President Zhang Youxia was removed from office in August 2026. Source: AFP / Ichiro Ohara/The Yomiuri Shimbun

He Weidong was removed as Vice Chairman of the CMC and Politburo member, and expelled from the Chinese Communist Party and the People's Liberation Army on 17 October, 2025.

The defence ministry said he was expelled over serious party discipline violations and suspected of serious duty-related crimes involving an "exceptionally large amount of money".

His expulsion made him the first serving uniformed Central Military Commission vice-chair to be removed since the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution.

title: Passport information may have been exposed in Flight Centre cyber incident
text:
In brief Flight Centre is investigating a data breach that may have exposed some customer information.

The incident has raised concerns about passport details and travel records being accessed.

Travel giant Flight Centre is investigating a data breach at one of its booking providers which may have exposed customer passport information.

The company is investigating "unusual activity" in a third-party accommodation booking system used by its brands, it said in a statement to the ASX on Thursday.

"[Flight Centre] is still working with the third-party vendor and [our] cybersecurity incident response partner ... to understand the nature and extent of the activity," the statement said.

Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings were not affected, the company said.

A significant number of customer records are believed to have been accessed by unknown persons, but the company said it did not know how many records had actually been extracted.

title: Plan to keep more Australian gas onshore set to become law after Labor, Coalition form deal
text:
In brief Labor had convinced the Coalition to strike a deal on its domestic gas reservation scheme.

It is hoped the scheme will deliver a "modest oversupply" of gas from 2028.

title: 'The costs are enormous': Behind some Australians' front doors is a $3.8 billion burden
text:
In brief A new report has described Australia's housing crunch as a public health crisis.

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

When housing and public health researcher Rebecca Bentley asks a room full of people if they've ever lived in a home with mould, she tends to get a similar response: most raise their hands.

"We do actually have a high tolerance for mould and damp in Australian homes because it's something we've grown to accept a bit," the University of Melbourne professor told SBS News.

But experts say that tolerance comes at a cost.

New research led by the university's Healthy Housing Unit estimates that eliminating household mould could save Australia $3.8 billion in healthcare expenditure and prevent $5.9 billion in lost income over the next 20 years.

And mould isn't the only hazard that could be harming Australians inside their own homes.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The research estimates that 2.5 million Australian households live in unhealthy homes, with issues such as poor ventilation, exposure to pollutants and toxins, pests and extreme indoor temperatures posing risks to occupants' health.

Its authors say high housing prices are pushing Australians into homes that don't meet their needs, with renters more likely to be exposed to poor-quality homes.

"We know that there's an affordability crisis in Australia. That housing supply is low. Rental affordability is not good in Australia at the moment," said Bentley, who is also director of the Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Housing.

"So all of these things contribute to this large burden of what we would describe as unhealthy housing in Australia."

How can unhealthy housing affect people?

Poor housing conditions can contribute to respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses and poor mental health, as well as affect children's development, productivity and life expectancy.

Bentley said the health consequences of household mould extend beyond physical conditions such as asthma, with exposure also taking a toll on people's mental health — something that was not factored into the modelling.

"So in fact, this estimate of $3.8 billion is actually a relatively conservative estimate," she said.

Distinguished professor Brian Oliver, who researches environmental health at the University of Technology Sydney, said the economic burden of household mould alone might surprise people.

"Even minor ailments cost money.

"It's not like if you've got mould in your bathroom, you're going to drop dead. But if you feel unwell, if you've got days off work, if you're visiting a healthcare practitioner, and if you've got chronic exposure and it leads to chronic disease, then the costs are enormous."

Some housing-related hazards are less visible, such as exposure to excessive noise.

Oliver said noise from busy roads or nearby industrial activity can disrupt residents' sleep, with long-term sleep deprivation linked to a range of health problems.

Living near busy roads can also affect the quality of the air residents breathe.

"Some people live next to busy roads, and they may as well be camping on the road because of the way that their houses work," Oliver told SBS News.

Recognising when your home is making you sick

Oliver said one potential indication that a person's home is affecting their health is if their symptoms improve when they spend time away from it.

He said it's also worth paying attention if a guest observes something about your home that you may have grown accustomed to.

"If you have someone come into your house, and they say, 'Oh, there's an unusual smell', or 'I don't feel so well', that's something you should definitely take notice of."

However, Oliver cautioned against becoming overly concerned about minor exposure to household hazards, noting that the level of exposure matters.

He said there are simple steps people can take to improve the health of their homes, such as opening a bathroom window or switching on an extractor fan after showering to reduce moisture build-up.

If you suspect your home is affecting your health, Oliver recommends speaking to a GP.

What can be done about unhealthy housing?

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

In particular, the report calls for stronger and more consistent protections for renters nationally, including minimum housing standards covering ventilation, indoor temperatures, repairs, mould and damp.

Roughly a third of the Australian population is renting, and that share is expected to expand over time.

"If renters don't feel like they will be evicted or their rent will be put up if they say ask for mould to be fixed in their home, that's another way in which we can just increase the probability that these problems will be addressed and reduced for people," Bentley said.

The report also calls for stronger construction regulations to improve the quality of new homes, including measures to reduce exposure to environmental noise and extreme indoor temperatures and minimise maintenance issues.

"The choice before us is clear. We can continue to meet the costs of unhealthy housing through hospitals, welfare systems, lost productivity and preventable suffering," Bentley said.

"Or we can invest upstream — in homes that keep people healthy, safe and secure."

title: One of Australia's most popular island escapes is running short of water
text:
IN BRIEF Fiji has declared a national state of disaster due to El Niño-induced water shortages.

Ninety-two communities across Fiji have no water supply, while 372 are at critical water levels.

Australian tourists holidaying in Fiji are being advised to take safety precautions over water, as thousands of locals in surrounding communities struggle to access reliable drinking water, with visitor numbers potentially straining resources further.

Fiji has declared a national state of disaster after an El Niño-driven drought caused widespread water shortages.

Almost 100 communities are now without water, while hundreds more are experiencing critically low supplies, according to the country's National Disaster controller Mitieli Cama.

In addition, Cama says 61 per cent of monitored water sources have reached critical levels.

Fiji has declared a national state of disaster in response to prolonged dry weather and worsening water shortages linked to El Niño conditions. Source: SIPA USA / Sang Qinlong

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Fiji's government says the conditions are likely to persist to the middle of next year.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka declared the state of disaster for one month to support "an intensified national response".

He urged people to conserve water, avoid unnecessary burning, and asked businesses to support the federal response.

"We cannot control the climate, but we can act early, use our resources responsibly and stand together through its impacts," he said in a national address last week.

The Fiji Sun reported that government agencies and partners were moving to restore water supplies to affected communities by accelerating emergency water carting, activating boreholes and using water treatment initiatives and alternative water sources.

READ MORE BoM issues a fresh 'super' El Niño reality check for Australia

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade issued new travel advice to Australians on Wednesday, saying tourists should exercise normal safety precautions.

"Water supplies may be impacted, and water rationing may be in place," a Smartraveller post said.

"Extended periods of dry weather may also affect food security and public health.

"Monitor weather conditions before you travel. Check with your travel provider or hotel for updates. Get travel insurance before you go and make sure you’re covered for the duration of your trip."

Fiji's National Disaster Risk Management Office has been helping supply water to communities. Credit: Fiji National Disaster Risk Management Office

But there are concerns growing tourism numbers may put further pressure on water and electricity supplies. Local media reports Fiji's hydroelectric dams could be shut down by the end of January 2027 if the dry conditions persist. It could force the country into expensive fuel-powered generation.

The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has told the Fiji Sun that visitor numbers could strain resources.

"Fiji’s tourism sector continues to record strong visitor numbers, but that growth also brings increasing demand on essential infrastructure," chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said.

"With approximately 800 additional rooms expected to come online next year, the demands on water and electricity supply will only increase."

In Papua New Guinea, around 680,000 people are expected to receive drought assistance from governmental and UN agencies, as extreme weather and water shortages put communities at risk.

The UN says El Niño is expected to peak in December, naming Papua New Guinea and Tonga as countries most at risk in the region, alongside Myanmar, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, causing weather extremes around the world, including drought in some regions and flooding in others. Some scientists say global warming may increase its intensity.

The US Climate Prediction Center said last week that El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 79 per cent chance of a strong-to-very-strong event through January to March. Australia said in June that El Niño could intensify in the second half of 2026 to become one of the strongest in seven decades.

Fiji's national weather bureau warned in October that strong El Niño conditions persist across the tropical Pacific.

Rainfall is likely to remain below normal from November through April, while daytime temperatures are expected to exceed normal levels through January across most of the country, the Fiji Meteorological Service said.

title: One Nation defector Leah Blyth accuses Liberals of infighting and lack of conviction
text:
In brief Leah Blyth criticised both the Coalition and Labor, saying One Nation would fight for the future of the country.

Her move marks the second defection by a Coalition member, after Barnaby Joyce joined One Nation last year.

South Australian senator Leah Blyth has taken aim at the Liberal Party while exiting the party, accusing it of abandoning its values and declaring One Nation the only party with the conviction to turn Australia "in the right direction".

Blyth, appointed to the Senate in February 2025 to replace retiring senator Simon Birmingham, became One Nation's fifth senator and the first from South Australia after she defected from the Liberals on Wednesday.

Flanked by her new One Nation colleagues at Parliament House on Thursday morning, Blyth said she had done her best to unite the Liberal Party as SA branch president.

But she said the party was plagued by "infighting" and that she did not feel safe, pointing out that she had hired private security to attend the SA branch's recent annual general meeting.

"I believe that One Nation is the only party that has the track record, the consistency, the courage, and the conviction to do what is right to get Australia heading in the right direction," she said.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson (centre) welcomed Leah Blyth's (second from left) decision to defect. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

"I no longer believed that the Liberal Party was the vehicle that was going to bring about the change that our country so desperately needs."

Blyth said the decision to quit was "mine alone" and she had not consulted her Liberal Party colleagues.

She took issue with the party over what she perceived as inconsistent policies, citing its pledge to abandon net zero while remaining in the Paris Agreement.

"My values have been constant and they have been consistent," she said.

"What has changed is the Liberal Party. They have abandoned their values, and so for me, I feel as though the Liberal Party left me, not the other way around."

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said Blyth was a "true conservative".

"This is a win for Australians, people that are fed up with the major political parties who have not listened to them and have not delivered for them," she said.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who defected from the Nationals nearly a year ago, said Blyth's defection was a "great endorsement of how One Nation is going".

One Nation becoming 'turncoat town'

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told reporters it was a "disappointing decision".

"The fact that she feels that the Liberal Party doesn't reflect her views anymore is a surprise to all of us. It's certainly not something that she ever mentioned in the party room. But she wasn't a big contributor to the party room," she said.

"I don't think it’s internal division. This is Leah's decision. She believes that she can make her contribution elsewhere. I think that the contribution can be made best by the Liberal Party.

"I think the highlight of this year has been seeing the fact that our team has really united, has gathered around, put its policy agenda out there."

Nationals leader Matt Canavan told reporters on Thursday the defection "smacks of self-interest" and One Nation was becoming "turncoat town".

"It's always disappointing to see someone leave a party that they were elected by," he said.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Leah Blyth's defection "smacked of self-interest". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"I think people see that as a defection, as a turncoat. And One Nation is becoming turncoat town right now, where they seem to be much more focused on taking people away from other political parties than changing the government and therefore changing the policy and changing the direction of this country."

He said he didn't buy Blyth's explanation that she joined One Nation due to its policies.

"It instead just smacks of self-interest; [she] went to the election last year supporting net zero," he said.

The defection comes after a Newspoll survey on Monday showed Labor and One Nation tied with 27 per cent of the primary vote, while the Coalition stood at 22 per cent — its highest level this year.

title: Donald Trump announces new tariffs on China, Japan and the EU
text:
In brief A previous tariff regime under national emergency laws was struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The new tariffs rely on a different court-tested trade law, with maximum rates of 20 to 40 per cent.

United States President Donald Trump has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

Australia was not among the countries affected.

His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting.

But the US Trade Representative's (USTR) office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.

In unveiling the results of an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices related to excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to further rebuild Trump's tariff leverage after the Supreme Court, in February, struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The effort also seeks to put Trump's tariffs and associated trade agreements on firmer legal and political grounds by backing them with a court-tested trade law, and by addressing foreign subsidies and industrial policies that are viewed as major trade problems by both Republicans and Democrats.

Separately, USTR proposed a new 10 per cent tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brazil to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempt from Trump's 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods, imposed in July as part of a separate investigation.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made "no meaningful progress".

China tops excess capacity rates

Under the excess factory capacity inquiry, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on 10 January. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent, the USTR said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with the US, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.

Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a 25 January public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.

The duties would not stack on top of prior tariffs of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent imposed under a separate US probe into lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 60 economies, nor would they add to national security duties on steel, aluminium, autos and other goods.

Greer said the proposed tariffs also would not apply to about US $30 billion ($45 billion) of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

The US has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

A spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China is a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called issue of 'industrial overcapacity' does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation," the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Lower rates for trade deals

The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 per cent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 per cent, including existing "Most Favoured Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.

India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail, the USTR said.

Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10 per cent.

Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.

"We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said, adding that the capped rates are no surprise to trading partners.

Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain underway, Greer said.

Trump's tariffs and their impact on rising living costs were a major issue in Democrats' sweeping victory in midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62 per cent of respondents supported efforts by Democrats to repeal them.

title: 'Incompetent': Bereaved parents lash Angus Taylor after generic email blunder
text:
In Brief Bereaved mothers say they felt "gaslit" after seeking support for stronger social media age limits.

Angus Taylor's office has not acknowledged the error, despite being alerted nearly two weeks ago.

This story contains references to suicide

Two bereaved families who advocate for children's online safety say they were "gaslit" by Opposition leader Angus Taylor after they spoke to him to seek support for stronger social media age limits, criticising his response as "incompetent" after receiving a delayed email referring to a different bill.

Online safety campaigners Mia Bannister and Emma Mason, who both had children that died following severe online harm, said they followed up their September meeting with Taylor with a passionate email asking for action. But his office's response three weeks later included a word-for-word copy of the Liberal Party’s website page about a different piece of legislation, they told SBS News.

Taylor's office then failed to acknowledge the mistake when SBS News highlighted the error 13 days ago and has not contacted the parents.

Bannister founded Ollie's Echo, a charity devoted to the memory of her son Ollie, who died by suicide in January 2024 aged 14 following sustained online bullying and a short battle with anorexia. She advocates against bullying, body image pressures, eating disorders, and online harms through school and community programs.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She and Mason met with Taylor's office on 8 September about why he should back changes to the social media minimum age bill.

The parents say they thought Taylor had listened, but his response indicated otherwise.

Two days later, Taylor voted against the changes to the social media minimum age bill, leaving the parents who met with him greatly disappointed and accusing him of politicising young people who have been harmed.

They sent him an email asking why he had voted against the changes and three weeks later, received an email stating the Coalition was opposed to the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 — a different bill to the one they had discussed with him. The email contained the same wording as the Liberal Party's website, on why the party would not support the digital duty of care bill, which passed the parliament on Wednesday, after Labor struck a deal with the Greens.

Communications Minister Anika Wells with bereaved parents Mia Bannister, Robb Evans, Emma Mason at Parliament House in July. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Bannister told SBS News she was "gobsmacked" that Taylor's email didn't address the issues they talked about during the meeting.

"At least [former Liberal leader] Peter Dutton showed some empathy when I met him," Bannister said. "Not once in this whole process has the Opposition reached out except for [Queensland MP] Andrew Wallace."

"Yes, we were in Canberra for the exposure draft for the digital duty of care. However, when we sat down with the leader of the Opposition and Andrew Wallace, we did not discuss the digital duty of care. We discussed the fact that they voted against the amendments to the social media minimum age legislation," Bannister said.

She said she felt Taylor was deliberately trying to lump the digital duty of care bill into his response because the Coalition did not support it.

"I hate these terms of gaslighting and ghosting ... [but] absolutely, it would be gaslighting us completely."

When Bannister gave evidence at the Digital Duty of Care Senate hearing earlier this month, Communication Minister Anika Wells' office "picked up the phone and thanked us again".

"I don't think the Coalition realise the toll it takes on us every time we have to get up and speak about our kids, but we do it because we feel if we stop, there's no one else driving it forward. So that's why we do what we do.

"I just found the leader of the Opposition very cold, whereas we've had very different experiences with other members of parliament. It was the Coalition that pushed for the social media laws in the first place, and then Labor took it on. So I find it actually extremely rude, and yes, incompetent."

Mason told SBS News it was "concerning" that the Coalition, which got the issue of child protection onto the national stage, "now decided that because of whatever's going on in their own political sphere, they need to do some point scoring".

"I spoke to [former Liberal leader] Sussan Ley, just before she resigned [in February this year] and we talked openly about the situation, and then there's just been crickets," Mason said.

"So it's very odd. And then, having actually reached out, [Taylor] writes an email that doesn't address what we were addressing; we correct that, and then again, no answer. I think intrinsically he's a good man. It's not malicious, but it's just odd."

Mason began campaigning for online safety after her 15-year-old daughter, Tilly Rosewarne, died by suicide in February 2022 following severe cyberbullying. Mason spoke at the United Nations in September 2025 urging global leaders to raise social media age limits and continues to push for safety online.

Taylor's office has been known to have communications mishaps in the past, including the 2019 "Fantastic. Great move. Well done Angus." social media blunder where he or someone in his office was found to be commenting on his Facebook posts and the controversy over incorrect travel figures used to attack Sydney lord mayor Clover Moore, which he blamed on his office.

A spokesperson for Taylor told SBS News their "hearts go out to every family who has lost a child", and they "strongly support laws that keep children safe online".

"That is why the Coalition led the way on the original social media minimum age legislation, which passed Parliament with bipartisan support," the spokesperson said.

"We want to see children better protected online. We consider that the best way to achieve this is through proper implementation of the social media ban, which, disappointingly, has, to date, only seen around a 5 per cent reduction in teens on social media.

"Mr Taylor held a constructive meeting on the legislation. The Coalition moved amendments to the Bill to address privacy concerns and strengthen safety, which the Government ultimately rejected.

"Our office will be in touch with Emma and Mia to fully outline the Coalition’s position on the Bill."

Bannister and Mason shared with SBS News the email chain to Taylor's office following the meeting. They expressed anger and disappointment and urged that they not be treated as "political props".

"We repeatedly pleaded with you to put politics aside and we meant it," their email read in part.

"We had hoped that was something we could count on both sides of Parliament to fight for with us. We remain profoundly disappointed that this was not the case."

title: Higher taxes on trusts set to become law after Labor secures Greens support
text:
In brief New laws will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts.

Private jet owners will have to pay the same fuel excise rate as motorists under the new laws.

Individuals and small businesses will have to pay higher taxes on trusts after the Greens gave the proposal the support it needs to pass the Senate.

The law, announced in the government's May budget, will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts, but will now also hit private jet owners with a higher fuel levy, as the minor party demanded.

Discretionary trusts can be used to split income, including among relatives and families running businesses — something critics argue is a way for the wealthy to dodge higher income taxes.

"Discretionary trusts are basically a legalised defrauding of the Commonwealth that is overwhelmingly exploited by super wealthy people to avoid paying their fair share," Greens treasury spokesperson Nick McKim told reporters on Wednesday.

"At the end of the day, today Australia's tax system will just be a little bit fairer, and it will be fairer because we are cracking down on the 1 per cent."

The Greens had hoped Labor would agree to close a loophole for non-taxpaying entities like private schools, religious institutions and sporting clubs, but the parties instead struck a deal.

The tax office would now be able to better target trust distributions to "cults" and charities without a deductible recipient endorsement, according to McKim.

"There will be extra resources for the ATO ... there will also be stronger probity frameworks that will be able to be enforced," he said.

Small businesses and industry groups had forecast a $1 billion hit if the changes took effect, pleading with the government to abandon the proposal amid a cost of living crisis.

The Business Council of Australia had said employers would be hit twice — once to comply with the new rules and a second time when they paid the higher tax.

The Coalition opposed the measures over businesses' concerns, leaving the Greens as Labor's sole negotiating partner in the upper house.

The trust tax concessions are the latest in a volley of recent wins for the minor party, who snagged changes to the government's digital duty of care laws on Tuesday and landed a deal to carve out pensioners from cuts to private health insurance rebates.

title: Implosion: The downfall of China’s money king
text:

The gala in Xiong’an was meant to be an extravagant affair. The host, CreditEase, a rare Chinese wealth manager with a stellar reputation, was turning 20. Its founder, Tang Ning, wanted to show his appreciation for the Communist Party, whose boss, Xi Jinping, handpicked Xiong’an as a big city-building project. The date was set for late May. Then the event was abruptly cancelled. CreditEase collapsed soon after. In October, Tang, his wife and many of his employees were detained. Earlier this month his firm’s 11-year-old New York-listed unit said it faced delisting.

The fiasco has shaken China’s investment industry. CreditEase was as trusted as such firms get in Chinese finance. It now owes some 100,000 clients $US4.4 billion ($6.6 billion) in principal. Its troubles add to a long list of implosions causing financial insecurity for millions of Chinese.

CreditEase chief Tang Ning, his wife and many of his employees were detained in October. AP

Founded in 2006, CreditEase was a pioneer of peer-to-peer (P2P) lending. It connected wealthy folk with cash to spare to others in need of it and willing to pay high interest rates, circumventing clunky state banks and helping discover true market prices for credit. Tang spawned thousands of imitators. Many lent to risky borrowers eschewed by banks. Some absconded with investors’ cash. In 2016 the state began tightening previously lax rules, and by 2020 most forms of P2P were banned. The majority of providers either collapsed or were wound down. Many bosses were detained.

Tang found a way to keep CreditEase going. The firm lent money to borrowers and then passed bundles of loans to intermediaries, which in turn packaged them into fixed-income products listed on provincial or municipal asset exchanges. These products’ guaranteed yield of 8 per cent over one to three years, making them popular with investors whose money made its way back to CreditEase. The firm then used the proceeds to make more loans. Passing through a public exchange legitimised the process. Tang’s links to officials in Beijing probably helped, too, says an insider.

One of modern football’s most successful partnerships has fractured, with Collingwood parting ways with list boss Justin Leppitsch following ongoing tensions with premiership coach Craig McRae. The Magpies confirmed Leppitsch’s immediate departure on Friday afternoon, bringing an abrupt end to a five-season tenure that helped deliver one of the most remarkable transformations in the club’s history. Magpies coach Craig McRae speaks with assistant Justin Leppitsch during the club’s 2023 premiership year. Getty Images The professional relationship between McRae and Leppitsch, forged when they were teammates in Brisbane’s era of supremacy at the turn of the century and then rekindled during Richmond’s premiership dynasty, was central to Collingwood’s renaissance. But the relationship that underpinned so much of Collingwood’s success has become increasingly strained, with Leppitsch’s departure the subject of speculation in senior football circles for some time.

Advertisement

Justin Leppitsch is on the move from Collingwood. AFL Photos The irony of Leppitsch’s exit is that two men who helped engineer Collingwood’s ascent to the summit of Australian football will no longer work together as the club confronts the complexities of sustaining that success. The timing of his departure is particularly significant given Collingwood finds itself at a delicate juncture in its list evolution, attempting to reconcile its immediate premiership ambitions with the inevitable generational change confronting its ageing playing group. In the short term, football general manager Charlie Gardiner will assume responsibility for list management while the Magpies determine the future structure of their football department. The relationship between a senior coach and a list manager is among the most consequential in any football club, particularly when the competing demands of immediate success and long-term sustainability become increasingly difficult to reconcile.

Advertisement

Collingwood’s unsuccessful pursuit of Richmond premiership defender Jayden Short during this year’s trade period came amid speculation about the relationship between McRae and Leppitsch. There was also scrutiny of Leppitsch’s public commentary surrounding the future of premiership midfielder Jordan De Goey, who comes out of contract at the end of next season. Craig McRae and Justin Leppitsch teamed up at Collingwood in the 2020s (main), Brisbane in the 2000s, with Michael Voss (top right) and at Richmond in the 2010s (bottom right). Getty Leppitsch subsequently confirmed during the trade period that both De Goey and rebounding defender Dan Houston would remain at Collingwood in 2027. The acquisitions of dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman medallist Jesse Hogan in October were the clearest indication yet that the Magpies believe their premiership window remains open.

Advertisement

Neither acquisition required Collingwood to sacrifice significant draft capital, allowing the club to supplement its existing group with established talent while retaining some capacity to invest in the next generation. Related Article AFL 2027 Suspended Swans return for AFL pre-season; Essendon build ruck depth at rookie draft On trade deadline night in October, Leppitsch talked of Collingwood’s controversial strategy of never wanting to allow their list to bottom out. “As a club, and [chief executive officer] Craig Kelly’s driven this, we don’t want empty stands. We want to give ourselves the ability to win consistently while nabbing a flag along the journey, as opposed to the longer path, which we all know what that is,” he said. “There might come a day where we have to do that … but we don’t feel like it’s in the near future.”

Advertisement

Whoever succeeds Leppitsch will inherit one of the more intriguing list management assignments in the competition: overseeing the transition away from some of the most accomplished players in Collingwood’s history while constructing a team capable of capitalising on the prime years of superstar midfielder Nick Daicos. Leppitsch initially joined the Magpies as an assistant coach ahead of the 2022 season before moving into strategy and innovation and eventually assuming responsibility for list management following the departure of former football boss Graham Wright. Wright, now chief executive of Carlton, was another of the central architects of Collingwood’s 2023 premiership. The Magpies have undergone considerable change in their football department since defeating Brisbane in that grand final, with Leppitsch the latest of the influential figures behind that triumph to depart the club.

Advertisement

“The 2023 premiership was no doubt a highlight, but I’d like to particularly thank our current list management and recruiting team – it has been a privilege to work alongside such talented and dedicated people,” Leppitsch said. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 No second chance: Why Buckley and Simpson were overlooked Leppitsch, who played in three consecutive premierships alongside McRae at Brisbane under Leigh Matthews, has accumulated considerable experience across almost every facet of a football department since his retirement as a player. He spent three seasons as senior coach of the Lions between 2014 and 2016 before returning to Richmond, where he was part of Damien Hardwick’s coaching team during the Tigers’ era of premiership dominance from 2017-20. His reunion with McRae at Collingwood in late 2021 represented the continuation of a professional association that spanned more than two decades.

In mid-October Will Cowper stood in the middle of Pici and surveyed his first restaurant as co-owner. It was very much a construction site. It was dirt floors and exposed framing and random equipment and all sorts of other gubbins strewn about the place. Downstairs, an earthmover sat silent behind a high-vis barrier mesh. Pici opens next week, Wednesday, December 2. Markus Ravik Five weeks later, Cowper sits in Pici and looks you dead in the eye, his ready smile dropping for a moment. “The last three weeks have probably been the hardest of my life. It’s been really difficult,” he says. “Now, it just feels surreal.”

Advertisement

Surreal because it’s over. Pici is finished. And it’s hard to believe it ever looked like a construction site, such is its sense of presence. It’s a real looker – absolutely a contender for the prettiest of the year. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article One of 2026’s best openings is from two chefs you’ve never heard of Cowper is opening the restaurant with his wife, pastry chef Gianna Cowper, and Andrew and Andrea Solomon, best known as co-operators of The Fish Factory. Cowper’s done this before. He opened Otto Brisbane – a restaurant he will long be associated with – at 480 Queen in 2016, and then moved with it to South Bank in 2021. “480 was similar because you’re coming up from Sydney, building a team from scratch,” he says. “But this has been a thought process about where things are, where things need to be. How are we going to do everything? How do we build the team? It’s a million little things.” Alkot Studio was in charge of the design. They’ve helped produce one of prettiest openings of the year. Matt Shea

Advertisement

The delay was caused by issues with some of the heritage aspects of the building. But the upshot was that once the green light reappeared, much of the build was ready to simply slot into place. It’s a venue of bold marble and rich dark timber and exposed brick and mirrored surfaces. Designers Alkot Studio have left the general layout similar to Gerties before it, with the bar up top and the dining space half a floor down on the Brunswick Street side. But then you remember that the Cowpers and Solomons knocked down the wall to what was Hellhound, giving Pici much more space. Pici’s kitchen sits on the lower floor that used to be shared by Gerties and Hellbound next door. Markus Ravik The open low-countered kitchen is on this floor, parked up against the back wall. Its eye-catching feature is a fairly hefty woodfire grill custom-made for Cowper by Sydney’s Platinum Commercial Kitchens. Pici’s menu will, as is standard nowadays, change with the seasons. Similar to Otto – and many a modern Australian Italian restaurant – it’s split into snacks, entrees, pastas and mains, but that’s where the similarity to Otto ends. No one would argue an on-form Otto is poor value, given the experience, but you wouldn’t say it’s cheap either.

Advertisement

Pici, on the other hand, is keenly priced. None of the entrees are more than $30, and most of the pastas hover about the $40 mark. It’s designed to encourage return visits from the locals. But it should also mean, very simply, that more people will now get to experience Cowper’s cooking, which is a nice thought. Champagne lobster ravioli with semi dried tomato ‘acqua pazza’ and basil. Markus Ravik On the bites menu there are dishes such as gnocco fritto with parmesan custard, prosciutto and saba syrup; fried baccala with an option to add caviar; and chargrilled Fremantle octopus skewers with padron peppers and a puttanesca sauce. For entrees you might order Noosa Red tomatoes with goat’s curd, olives, pickled onion, basil and focaccia; raw Mooloolaba yellowfin tuna; or Cowper’s take on a classic Piedmontese vitello tonnato. Char-grilled Fremantle octopus skewer with padron peppers and puttanesca sauce. Matt Shea

Advertisement

The five pastas include champagne lobster ravioli with a semi-dried tomato acqua pazza and basil; pork and fennel sausage pici with a white ragu, cime di rapa and chilli; and Longreach lamb shoulder fettuccine with green olive, peas and salted ricotta. For mains, there’s market fish served with an almond cream and salsa verde; Gooralie pork loin with grilled peach and a mustard sauce; and a 200-gram Stone Axe Wagyu flank with mushroom butter and veal sauce. Buffalo mozzarella with capsicum, capers, olives, basil and red wine vinegar. Markus Ravik Gianna Cowper’s Swiss-precise deserts are presented in a more stripped back fashion here. The menu includes chocolate mousse with cherry and a stracciatella gelato, a neatly presented take on tiramisu, and a vanilla bean ice cream affogato, to which you can add a shot of Nocello. For wines, Cowper tapped Cork and Co’s Chris Fullerton and Logan Moore to lay out a list that for most part keeps things under $100. It prioritises Italian drops, but also features French wines and Australian wines in an Italian style.

Advertisement

Fried baccala with creme fraiche and caviar. Matt Shea There’s also a clutch of classic cocktails and some originals and twists by bar manager Ellery Low (who many will recognise from his years at Maker in Fish Lane). Talking Low, he’s a brilliant hire for the Cowpers and Solomons. But he’s not the only one. There’s also Brendon Osmers (Alice, Gerard’s Bar, The Gresham et al) working next to Low, Marieke Ameglio (Sasso Italiano) running front-of-house, and Jack Burgess (formerly Venner) in the kitchen as Cowper’s sous chef. Pici’s bar is overseen by Ellery Low and Brendon Osmers. Markus Ravik It’s a real Murderers’ Row of talent but, also, they’re all very recognisable, hospitality-forward people, and it adds to the restaurant’s assured sense of family and community.

“We have our family and friends dinner tonight, of course,” Cowper says. “It will just be our nearest and dearest. It’s going to be a time to reflect and go, ‘F---, this is our restaurant.’ And it’s beautiful and everything I ever worked for, and we’re finally here.” Open Wed 5.30pm-10pm, Thu 12pm-10pm, Fri 12pm-11pm, Sat 11.30am-11pm, Sun 11.30am-10pm. 699 Brunswick Street, New Farm, (07) 3835 8503. picirestaurantbar.com.au

Sophie Quick November 27, 2026 — 5:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. I’ve just come back from a week away on holiday and I’ve realised that, unfortunately, when I’m at an airport, I can’t completely recognise the full humanity of other people. I am the Main Character, containing multitudes, and everyone I encounter is either an angel or an antagonist depending on whether they are helping or hindering me as I navigate the terminal. Angel: the security guy pointing out the sunglasses I almost left on the x-ray tray. Antagonist: the high-heeled lady with her portable scales, fat-shaming my suitcase at the departure gate. Angel: the woman who shifted her seat so we could both use a phone-charging port in the food court. Antagonist: child watching Paw Patrol at full volume. For everyone else, I feel nothing at all. It’s all about me – my needs, my departure time – until I have reached my destination, when I can (hopefully) snap back into regular form. Photo: Robin Cowcher I don’t think I’m the only one who feels this chilling effect at the airport. There are a few obvious reasons for it. You have to focus in the terminal because you’ll lose a lot of money if you miss your flight. The atmosphere of biometric surveillance – where every person is reduced to scannable data – is surely part of it too. Proximity to Qantas employees causes knock-on morale issues. (This is a shame. Hostility towards the executive leadership team running our national carrier should energise and unite all non-Qantas executive Australians! Sadly it just makes most of us tired.)

Advertisement

On screen, depictions of airports veer towards extremes. On one hand, airport terminals are sometimes treated as homogenous, transient “non-places”. (I’m thinking, especially, of the George Clooney movie Up in the Air). Or they’re places of high emotion and high stakes (from Home Alone, Love Actually and Carry On to reality TV shows like Border Security). My own experience tends more towards the first version, and I think that’s because I have not (yet) presented to an airport with humanitarian needs, access requests, urgent romantic confessions or smuggling objectives. Related Article Allergies Bless me (sniff), for I have endured the season of sinus congestion The modern airport experience is catered to people like me: able-bodied, digitally literate and English-speaking. Airlines would like to discourage human needs and human complications because they don’t want to pay human beings to deal with those things. I think their bad faith is rubbing off on me. Perhaps I should take inspiration from on-screen airport workers. Earlier this year, I binged the SBS hit series The Airport Chaplain (starring Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez). I’m now watching the 2024 comedy series How Not To Die Alone, set in JFK Airport (starring Natasha Rothwell). The first of these – about a chaplain who provides “emotional, spiritual and practical support” for passengers passing through the fictional Victoria Airport – falls firmly in the camp of high-stakes, high-emotion airport drama. How Not to Die Alone is more of a workplace comedy. They are both great series that dramatise complex workplace dynamics. And they’re both good reminders that while I – and many other passengers – may act like robots during our transient airport hours, there’s a lot going on for others, including the people who work there every day. Many airport jobs are, of course, highly exposed to economic instability and automation.

Advertisement

There’s a lot going on behind closed doors, too. My favourite thing about both these shows – and even about Border Security – is the scenes showing the bizarre variety of seized and surrendered goods in the restricted zone. In The Airport Chaplain there’s a storyline, based on a true story from Melbourne Airport, where a passenger tries to pass through security with live exotic fish hidden in plastic bags strapped to her legs. In How Not to Die Alone, Mel and her friend go looking in the surrendered items department for prescription painkillers and discover a $4000 luxury ham. In real life, I’m very grateful to the people who stop dangerous stuff getting onto planes or through customs. I’m glad they do what they do. But on a less practical level, it’s nice to reflect on how weird and unpredictable people are – especially in the dehumanising environment of the airport. In the departure hall, it’s all touchscreen kiosks and WHSmith. But the restricted security zone is a world of mystery fluids, experimental dairy products and confiscated frogs. It’s a world of bonkers human fetish and conspiracy. I’ll try to keep that in mind next time I enter an airport terminal and feel myself slipping into Main Character mode. It’s not just me who contains multitudes. Other passengers contain multitudes (of tropical fish in their pants, possibly) and I might be standing next to one of them.

The S&P/ASX200 rose 69.8 points on Friday, up 0.8 per cent, to 8833.6, as the broader All Ordinaries gained 77.6 points, or 0.88 per cent, to 8943.7. AI stocks boosted global indexes overnight. Reuters The local bourse has reclaimed roughly half the previous week’s losses after the reinstatement of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang helped temper artificial intelligence fears, but elevated oil prices, interest rates and global growth worries continue to cloud the earnings outlook. Only healthcare and utilities stocks ended lower in the week’s final session, with strong upswings in raw materials, energy and IT stocks.

Australia’s biggest tech company, WiseTech, jumped 15.08 per cent after releasing a bullish trading update. The company said it was confident it would reach its revenue guidance as its cost-savings drive was paying off. The rest of the tech sector was more muted. Xero plateaued, NEXTDC gained 2.47 per cent, Technology One slid marginally, and Codan closed 2.1 per cent higher. After initially sliding lower in early trade, mining stocks added to Thursday’s gains. BHP closed nearly 2 per cent higher, Rio Tinto was up 1.5 per cent, and Fortescue 1.88 per cent. Despite the price of gold slipping to hover near a 15-month low, Northern Star and fellow yellow metal producer Evolution Mining surged higher. Energy stocks advanced as oil prices rose again, tracking to their first weekly gain (of nearly 5 per cent) this month as attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers in the Middle East raise concerns about escalating hostilities. Brent crude closed above $US96 after Tehran-backed Houthi militants attacked Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on the Red Sea, temporarily halting some operations. They also targeted its Ras Tanura oil hub in the Persian Gulf earlier this week. The news boosted local energy stocks, with both Woodside and Santos adding 1.75 per cent, helping lift the bourse.

Banking stocks ended the week stable. Macquarie Group announced a shake-up on Friday morning of its banking arm. Amy Mahony will replace Stuart Green as Macquarie Bank’s chief executive and Tony Graham will take over Nicole Sorbara’s technology responsibilities and become the bank’s chief information officer. Overnight, the Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7 per cent as European indexes took centre stage with Wall Street closed for Thanksgiving. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.7 per cent. Technology shares led gains in many markets. Memory giants SK Hynix and Kioxia Holdings outperformed in Asia. Taiwan and South Korea’s technology-focused benchmarks rose more than 2 per cent. While Europe’s rally was led by auto and mining stocks, the region’s technology sector climbed more than 2 per cent.

The return of buyers to the artificial intelligence trade offers an encouraging sign after a bruising November. Markets have whipsawed since the US midterms, with a leadership crisis at Nvidia deepening a sell-off that pushed major gauges into corrections. “AI capex remains intact, financing is still readily available, and pricing power is exceptional,” said Marija Veitmane at State Street Global Markets. “Sentiment cracked, fundamentals didn’t. With tech valuations looking increasingly attractive, the sell-off may be starting to create its own reversal.” European bonds fell on waning demand for havens. Meanwhile, Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become European Central Bank president when Christine Lagarde leaves in February. For Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum, caution remains warranted for stocks, especially because there was no clear catalyst for the tech rebound. The likelihood of a US interest rate hike next month threatens to push the cost of capital even higher, adding to headwinds for the AI trade. “It’s a real mystery why dip buyers emerged,” Klement said. “Friday will be the real test if the recovery has staying power.”

Altria also said that it was in talks with another party over part of the British company’s business, as Japan Tobacco also was reported to be weighing a bid.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
